candidates.title: Surface Coating of Plastic Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you apply a material to a plastic substrate for purposes that include bonding (i.e., adhesives), decorative, protective, or functional purposes, then that activity is a surface coating of plastic parts and products and falls within the source category addressed by this subpart.

If your affected source uses 378 liters (100 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain hazardous air pollutants (HAP) in the surface coating of plastic parts and products and the source is a major source (or is located at or is part of a major source of HAP), then the subpart applies to that affected source.

If your facility does not use 378 liters (100 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain HAP for surface coating of plastic parts and products and the facility is not a major source (nor located at or part of a major source), then the subpart does not apply on that basis.

If the surface coating or coating operation meets any of the exemption criteria listed in paragraphs (c)(1) through (c)(17) of §63.4481 (for example: uses only coatings/thinners/cleaning materials with no organic HAP, is a research/laboratory/hobby activity, falls under another specific subpart by product or process, etc.), then that surface coating or coating operation is not subject to this subpart.

If the operations in question are part of the affected source as defined (all coating operations; all storage containers and mixing vessels for coatings/thinners/additives/cleaning materials; all equipment and containers used to convey coatings/thinners/additives/cleaning materials; and all storage and conveying equipment for waste generated by a coating operation), then those items constitute the affected source for applicability and compliance under this subpart.

If you commenced construction after December 4, 2002 by installing new coating equipment used to coat plastic parts where no such surface coating was previously performed at the source, or you commenced construction after December 4, 2002 to perform coating in a subcategory not previously performed, then the affected source is a new source for purposes of this subpart.

If the material you apply is a reactive adhesive in which at least 70 percent of the liquid components (excluding water) react during curing and those HAP react to form solids and are not emitted, then the organic HAP content (for purposes of determining compliance under this subpart) is the mass of organic HAP that is actually emitted rather than the mass received in the material.

checklist: Is the methylene chloride being applied for the purpose of bonding plastic parts (i.e., is the operation an adhesive application) or is it being used as a cleaning material or some other non-coating purpose? (determine intended use/purpose and how the material is applied).
Does the applied material meet the regulatory definition of a coating or adhesive (see definitions in 40 CFR 63.4581)?

What is the annual quantity (liters or gallons per year) of coatings that contain HAP used in the plastic parts surface coating activities (count only materials that meet the subpart's definition of coatings for the 378 L / 100 gal threshold)?

Is the facility a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥ 9.07 Mg (10 tons) of any single HAP per year or ≥ 22.68 Mg (25 tons) of combined HAP per year), or is the coating operation located at or part of such a major source?

Do any of the exemptions in §63.4481(c)(1)–(17) apply to your operation (e.g., you use only non-organic-HAP coatings; the activity is a research/lab, janitorial, or hobby shop; the operation is covered by another specific subpart; the coating is extrusion-applied plastic; etc.)? Verify each potentially relevant paragraph.
Are the storage, mixing, conveying, and waste-handling units associated with these activities included at your site and therefore part of the affected source as defined in §63.4482(b)?

Was the coating equipment installed (construction commenced) after December 4, 2002, and if so, was it installed where plastic surface coating was not previously performed or in a new subcategory, to determine new vs existing source status?

If you claim the material is a reactive adhesive with HAP that react into solids and are not emitted, do you have formulation data, test data, or other documentation to support that at least 70% of liquid components react and that emissions are correspondingly reduced (to use the reactive-adhesive provisions)?

judge_text: {"score":1, "reason":"The answer includes the EPA point that MeCl used to bond parts is an adhesive/coating (cites §63.4581), but it does not include the EPA’s crucial rationale that because no coating solids remain the §63.4490 limit (lb HAP per lb solids) cannot be determined and thus the subpart is not applied; the answer’s reactive‑adhesive criterion addresses adhesives that form solids (≥70% react) and does not capture the ‘no solids left’ basis for non‑application."}

candidates.title: Area source NESHAP for secondary copper smelters

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a new secondary copper smelter that is an area source of hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions, then you are subject to this subpart.

If your facility processes copper scrap in a blast furnace and converter or uses another pyrometallurgical purification process to produce anode copper from copper scrap, then the facility is a 'secondary copper smelter' (and falls within the subpart's subject definition).

If your facility merely melts recycled copper scrap or copper alloy scrap to produce ingots or for direct use in a manufacturing process, then the facility is not a 'secondary copper smelter' (and is not subject under that definition).
If you commenced construction or reconstruction of the affected source on or after October 6, 2006, then the secondary copper smelter is a new affected source for purposes of this subpart.
If your facility is a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7), then this subpart does not apply to your facility.

checklist: Is the product you cast anode copper intended to be refined in an electrolytic process (i.e., 'anode copper')?

Does your process use a pyrometallurgical purification route (e.g., smelting furnace, use of fluxes, oxidation/reduction steps, generation of slag) rather than only melting to make ingots or feedstock for direct manufacture?
Do you operate a smelting furnace or melting furnace defined as a vessel in which copper scrap and fluxes are melted to form a molten mass containing copper and slag?
Was construction or reconstruction of the affected source commenced on or after October 6, 2006?
Is the facility an area source of HAPs (based on potential to emit and permitting status) rather than a major source?
Is the facility a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7)?

judge_text: {"score": 2, "reason": "Yes — the answer includes the two key EPA points: (1) the anode furnace is a pyrometallurgical purification process producing anode copper from scrap and thus meets the 40 CFR 63.11158 definition of a secondary copper smelter, and (2) a new area source is subject under 40 CFR 63.11153(a)-(b). These criteria and corresponding checklist items are present in the submission."}

candidates.title: National Perchloroethylene Air Emission Standards for Dry Cleaning Facilities

criteria.criterion: If a dry cleaning facility uses perchloroethylene (PCE), then the provisions of this subpart apply to the owner or operator of that facility.
If a dry cleaning system is located in a building with a residence, then after December 21, 2020 the owner or operator shall eliminate any emission of PCE from that dry cleaning system.

If a dry cleaning system is installed (including relocation of a used machine) after December 21, 2005 and is located in a building with a residence, then the owner or operator shall eliminate any emission of PCE from that dry cleaning system upon installation.

If the total yearly PCE consumption of a dry cleaning facility is less than 530 liters (140 gallons) per year as determined under §63.323(d), then certain existing dry-to-dry and transfer machine facilities are exempt from many provisions of §§63.322, 63.323, and 63.324 but remain subject to the specific provisions listed (including §63.322(o)(5)(i)).

If the total yearly PCE consumption of a dry cleaning facility that includes only transfer machine system(s) is less than 760 liters (200 gallons) per year as determined under §63.323(d), then that facility is exempt from many provisions of §§63.322, 63.323, and 63.324 but remains subject to the specific provisions listed (including §63.322(o)(5)(i)).
If a dry cleaning machine is coin-operated, then it is exempt from the requirements of this subpart.
If the building contains short-term housing occupied by the same person for less than 180 days, then that space is excluded from the definition of 'residence' for purposes of this subpart.

If a facility is located in a building with a residence (even if the residence is vacant at the time), then the owner/operator must indicate that fact in the compliance notification required by §63.324(f).

checklist: Do you use perchloroethylene (PCE) in any machine at this facility? (40 CFR 63.320(a))

Is the dry cleaning machine located in a building that contains a residence (dwelling) above or adjacent to the shop, even if the residence is currently unoccupied? (40 CFR 63.322(o)(5)(i); 40 CFR 63.324(f)(3))
Is the housing above the shop 'short-term housing' occupied by the same person for less than 180 days (if yes, it is excluded from 'residence')? (40 CFR 63.321)
What is the construction/installation or reconstruction date of the dry cleaning machine (commenced before/after Dec 9, 1991; Dec 21, 2005; July 27, 2006)? (40 CFR 63.320(b), 40 CFR 63.322(o)(4))
Is the machine coin-operated? (coin-operated machines are exempt) (40 CFR 63.320(j))
Is the machine a dry-to-dry machine or a transfer machine system? (40 CFR 63.321 definitions; applicability/exemptions differ)

Calculate total yearly PCE consumption by summing purchases for the previous 12 months on the first day of each month per §63.323(d); compare against thresholds: 530 L (140 gal), 760 L (200 gal), 6,800 L (1,800 gal), and 8,000 L (2,100 gal). (40 CFR 63.323(d); 40 CFR 63.320(d),(e),(g))

Have you submitted the notifications required by §63.324 (initial notification, notification of compliance status), and did those notifications disclose whether the facility is located in a building with a residence (required by §63.324(f))? (40 CFR 63.324(a),(b),(f))

If you assert exemption based on low PCE consumption, do you have purchase receipts and the 12-month consumption log to document the exemption per §63.324(d) and the calculation method in §63.323(d)? (40 CFR 63.324(d); 40 CFR 63.323(d))

If subject to the engineering/control requirements, does the machine meet the specific emission-elimination or control-device requirements (refrigerated condenser, carbon adsorber, vapor barrier/vapor enclosure) and the applicable monitoring/inspection schedules? (40 CFR 63.322(a),(b),(o); 40 CFR 63.323)

judge_text: {"score": 1, "reason": "The answer captures the key point that a co-located residence counts even if unoccupied (it cites §63.322(o)(5)(i) and asks about an unoccupied residence). However it does not explicitly capture the EPA’s separate point that the December 21, 2020 requirement applies so long as a PCE machine remains in the building regardless of whether the machine is currently operating/idle; the criteria focus on use and consumption thresholds but do not state that mere presence of a PCE machine in the building (even if not in use) triggers the §63.322(o)(5)(i) requirement."}

candidates.title: Metal Fabrication and Finishing Area Sources (NESHAP)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an area source that is primarily engaged in the operations in one of the nine metal fabrication and finishing source categories listed in § 63.11514(a)(1)–(9) then you are subject to this subpart.
If you use materials that contain MFHAP or have the potential to emit MFHAP then the provisions of this subpart apply to each new and existing affected source as described in § 63.11514(b).

If you perform dry abrasive blasting, machining, dry grinding and dry polishing with machines, spray-applied painting, or welding operations that use materials containing MFHAP or have the potential to emit MFHAP then those operations constitute an affected source under this subpart.
If your facility is a research or laboratory facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7) then this subpart does not apply to you.
If the operations are tool or equipment repair operations, facility maintenance, or quality control activities as defined in § 63.11522 then this subpart does not apply to those operations.

If the operations are performed on-site at installations owned or operated by the Armed Forces of the United States, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or the National Nuclear Security Administration then this subpart does not apply.

If the operations produce military munitions manufactured by or for the Armed Forces or equipment directly and exclusively used to transport military munitions then this subpart does not apply to those operations.

If your welding affected source uses 2,000 pounds or more per year of welding rod containing one or more MFHAP (calculated on a rolling 12-month basis) then you must comply with the additional welding management practices and monitoring requirements in § 63.11516(f)(3)–(8).
If you spray-apply paints that contain MFHAP then you must follow the spray painting MFHAP control, spray booth/filter, spray equipment, and worker training requirements in § 63.11516(d).

If construction or reconstruction of the affected source commenced before April 3, 2008 then the affected source is an existing source, and if construction or reconstruction commenced on or after April 3, 2008 then it is a new source (relevant for compliance dates and deadlines).

checklist: Confirm the facility is an area source of HAP (not a major source).

Identify which of the nine metal fabrication and finishing source categories (§63.11514(a)(1)–(9)) best describes your primary operations (e.g., Electrical and Electronic Equipment Finishing Operations, Fabricated Metal Products, etc.).

Calculate whether production of the product(s) in that category represents at least 50% of facility production over the previous continuous 12 months to determine 'primarily engaged' status (see definition of 'primarily engaged' in §63.11522).
List all processes performed at the facility and confirm presence/absence of: dry abrasive blasting, machining, dry grinding/dry polishing with machines, spray-applied painting, and welding.

For every material, coating, welding rod, and abrasive used, obtain manufacturer/supplier formulation data or MSDS and determine concentrations of cadmium, chromium, lead, nickel (≥0.1% by weight) and manganese (≥1.0% by weight) to determine if materials 'contain MFHAP'.

For spray painting operations: verify whether paints applied are spray-applied; whether paints contain MFHAP; whether spray booths/rooms have appropriate enclosure and filters meeting ≥98% MFHAP capture (or waterwash alternative); and whether application equipment is HVLP or equivalent and painters are trained/certified per §63.11516(d).

For abrasive blasting: identify whether blasting is 'dry abrasive blasting', whether enclosures are totally enclosed/unvented or vented, whether filtration control devices are used, and whether blasted items exceed 8 ft in any dimension.

For welding: determine welding rod MFHAP content and rolling 12‑month welding rod usage in pounds to check the 2,000 lb/yr threshold; identify any fume capture/control systems and maintain manufacturer's specifications.

Determine whether any activities at the facility qualify as research/laboratory facilities, tool/equipment repair, facility maintenance, or quality control activities as defined in §63.11522 (these may be excluded).
Confirm whether operations occur at or for Armed Forces, NASA, or NNSA installations or involve production of military munitions (exemptions in §63.11514(g)–(h)).
Verify the date construction or reconstruction of the affected source began to determine new vs existing status relative to April 3, 2008.

If subject, prepare to gather and retain records and submit notifications/reports per §63.11519 (initial notification, notification of compliance status, and annual certification and compliance reports).

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"Our Answer includes the central applicability criterion (must be 'primarily engaged' in one of the nine §63.11514(a) categories and how to determine 'primarily engaged'), but it fails to capture the specific NAICS/SIC mapping rationale EPA used — i.e., that NAICS 335999 is paired with SIC 3699 (not SIC 3679) and therefore the facility falls outside the listed categories. The NAICS/SIC mapping check is not present in the criteria/checklist."}

candidates.title: Lime Manufacturing Plants

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a lime manufacturing plant (LMP) that is a major source of HAP, then you are subject to this subpart.

If the LMP is located at a kraft pulp mill, soda pulp mill, sulfite pulp mill, beet sugar manufacturing plant, or only processes sludge containing calcium carbonate from water softening processes, then the LMP is not subject to this subpart.

If the emission unit is a lime kiln used to produce a lime product from stone feed by calcination at an LMP that is a major source, then the lime kiln (and, for PM requirements, its associated cooler) and the processed stone handling (PSH) operations at that LMP are covered by this subpart.
If the equipment is a lime hydrator (device used to produce hydrated lime/calcium hydroxide), then that equipment is not subject to this subpart.

checklist: Determine whether the plant is a major source of HAP (any single HAP ≥ 9.07 Mg/yr [10 tpy] or total HAPs ≥ 22.68 Mg/yr [25 tpy]) at the plant site.

Confirm whether the facility 'uses a lime kiln to produce lime product from limestone or other calcareous material by calcination' (identify kiln feedstock: limestone, dolomite, shells, processed stone, or other calcareous substances such as calcium carbonate lime mud).

Document whether the kiln operation is limited to recalcining internally generated lime mud from a caustic recovery loop versus processing raw/processed stone feed, and whether the product is ‘lime product’ (quicklime/dead-burned lime).

Verify the facility type and location to see if it is colocated at an excluded facility type (kraft pulp mill, soda pulp mill, sulfite pulp mill, beet sugar manufacturing plant) or only processes water-softening sludge containing calcium carbonate.
Identify whether the unit in question is a lime kiln (including any associated preheater) versus a lime hydrator or other noncovered equipment.

Inventory whether associated lime coolers and processed stone handling (storage bins, conveyors, transfer points, bucket elevators, screening, surge bins, bulk loading/unloading) exist at the plant and their construction/reconstruction dates (to determine new vs existing status if needed).

judge_text: {"score": 1, "reason": "Some key EPA points are captured (the criteria and checklist explicitly address that calcining calcium carbonate lime mud constitutes a lime manufacturing plant and list the specific regulatory exclusions—kraft/soda/sulfite pulp mills, beet sugar, and water‑softening sludge—so a soda ash plant recovery loop is not exempt). However the EPA note that the rule does not require the lime to be sold (i.e., recalcining internally generated lime mud still falls within the rule even if product is retained onsite) is not explicitly stated in the criteria/checklist."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Reciprocating Internal Combustion Engines (RICE)

criteria.criterion: If you operate existing non-emergency four-stroke lean-burn (4SLB) or four-stroke rich-burn (4SRB) stationary RICE with a site rating of more than 500 HP located at an area source of HAP that are not remote stationary RICE and that are operated more than 24 hours per calendar year, then the initial compliance demonstration must be conducted according to the performance testing requirements in §63.6630(e).

If a stationary RICE meets the definition of remote stationary RICE in §63.6675, then the initial compliance testing requirements in §63.6630(e) that apply to non-remote >500 HP, area-source 4SLB/4SRB engines do not apply to those remote engines (i.e., §63.6630(e) is specified for engines that are not remote).

If you own or operate an existing stationary RICE located at an area source of HAP emissions, then you must submit the notifications listed in §§63.7(b) and (c), 63.8(e), 63.9(b) through (e), and (g) and (h) that apply to you by the dates specified, per §63.6645(a).

If an initial compliance demonstration required in Table 5 to this subpart does not include a performance test, then you must submit the Notification of Compliance Status before the close of business on the 30th day following completion of that initial compliance demonstration as specified in §63.6645(h)(1).

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If an affected source becomes subject to a relevant standard, then the owner or operator must submit an initial notification to the Administrator in writing not later than 120 calendar days after the effective date of the relevant standard (or within 120 days after the source becomes subject), per §63.9(b)(2).

If a State has been delegated authority to implement and enforce notification requirements under this part, then notifications must be submitted to the delegated State authority and a copy sent to the appropriate EPA Regional Office as specified in §63.9(a)(4)(ii); otherwise, submit notifications to the EPA Regional Office per §63.9(a)(4)(i).

If you send the Administrator a copy of a notice that you sent to the State and that copy contains all the information required in a notification listed in this section, then that copy may satisfy the requirements of §63.9, per §63.9(a)(3).

If a Notification of Compliance Status is required under this part, then the notification must be submitted before the close of business on the 60th day following completion of the relevant compliance demonstration activity (or before the close of business on the 30th day for demonstrations that do not include a performance test), per §63.9(h)(2) and as cross-referenced in §63.6645(h).

checklist: Document engine type for each unit (confirm four-stroke and whether lean-burn or rich-burn).
Record site rating (brake HP) for each engine (confirm each is 800 hp).
Confirm each engine is an existing unit (startup date relative to relevant effective dates).
Determine whether each engine is operated as a non-emergency engine (verify emergency vs non-emergency operation and hours criteria in §63.6640(f) if claiming emergency status).
Calculate annual operating hours for each engine (is operation >24 hours per calendar year for each engine?).

Determine whether each engine meets the 'remote stationary RICE' definition in §63.6675 by applying the geographic tests: count buildings intended for human occupancy within a 0.25 mile radius (or pipeline-segment tests where applicable), check for any buildings with four or more stories, and measure distances to nearby buildings or populated outdoor areas per the definition.

Document the date(s) when the geographic (remote) criteria were first met (you stated October 2013) and retain evidence (maps, surveys, photographs, or other records supporting the building counts and distances).

Verify whether the engines are located on a pipeline segment and, if so, apply the pipeline-segment criteria in §63.6675(2)(i)-(iii) (count buildings per continuous 1-mile segment and distances to buildings/outdoor areas).
Check whether you submitted any initial notifications or other notifications to the State or EPA required by §63.6645(a) and §63.9(b); obtain dates and copies of submissions (if any).

If no notification of remote status was submitted to the State or EPA, determine whether your State has delegation of §63.9 notification authority (so notifications should be sent to the State) per §63.9(a)(4), and whether a copy of any State notice could satisfy federal requirements per §63.9(a)(3).

Decide which initial compliance demonstration applies (performance test per §63.6630(e) for non-remote >500 HP 4SLB/4SRB engines operated >24 hr/yr, or an alternative demonstration for remote engines) and identify the applicable reporting deadline for the Notification of Compliance Status (30 days for demonstrations without a performance test per §63.6645(h)(1) or 60 days for those with a performance test per §63.6645(h)(2)/§63.9(h)(2)).

Gather documentation to support any claim that engines are 'remote' (engine location maps, building counts, distances, and any contemporaneous records showing when remote conditions were met) to be able to rely on exclusions from §63.6630(e).

judge_text: {"score": 1, "reason": "Some EPA key points are in the criteria (references to remote-definition §63.6675 and state delegation/notification rules §63.9 are present), but the answer does not capture two key reasons from the EPA notes: it fails to cite the annual evaluation/recordkeeping requirement for remote status (40 CFR 63.6603(f)) and does not clearly reflect EPA’s statement that no separate notification of remote status is required for existing non‑emergency >500 hp 4SLB/4SRB engines at area sources (the answer instead emphasizes general notification requirements, which could imply the opposite)."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Gasoline Dispensing Facilities

criteria.criterion: If a stationary facility dispenses gasoline into the fuel tank of a motor vehicle, motor vehicle engine, nonroad vehicle, or nonroad engine (i.e., meets the definition of a gasoline dispensing facility (GDF)) and the facility is located at an area source, then the affected source is subject to this subpart.

If the emission source consists of gasoline storage tanks and associated equipment components in vapor or liquid gasoline service at a GDF, then those storage tanks and associated components are covered by this subpart.
If the GDF's monthly throughput of gasoline is less than 10,000 gallons, then the facility must comply with the requirements in §63.11116 (and not the higher-throughput provisions).
If the GDF's monthly throughput of gasoline is 10,000 gallons or more, then the facility must comply with the requirements in §63.11117, and if 100,000 gallons or more then §63.11118 applies.
If the specific piece of equipment is the equipment used for the refueling of motor vehicles (as opposed to the gasoline storage tanks themselves), then that equipment is not covered by this subpart.

If gasoline is dispensed from a fixed gasoline storage tank at a GDF into a portable gasoline tank for on-site delivery and subsequent dispensing into a motor vehicle fuel tank, then that activity is subject only to §63.11116.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Area Source Standards for Bulk Gasoline Terminals, Pipeline Breakout Stations, Pipeline Pumping Stations, and Bulk Gasoline Plants

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a bulk gasoline terminal, pipeline breakout station, pipeline pumping station, or bulk gasoline plant (as identified in 63.11081(a)(1)–(4)) and the facility is an area source, then you are subject to this subpart.

If gasoline storage tanks are located at a bulk gasoline terminal/plant/pipeline station but are used only for dispensing gasoline in a manner consistent with tanks located at a gasoline dispensing facility (GDF), then those tanks are not subject to this subpart and instead must comply with subpart CCCCCC.
If storage tanks are used to load gasoline into a cargo tank for on-site redistribution to another storage tank, then those storage tanks are subject to this subpart.

checklist: For each tank, confirm the stored fuel type (gasoline vs diesel); if gasoline, determine whether its Reid vapor pressure is ≥ 27.6 kPa to meet the subpart CCCCCC definition of 'gasoline' (per 40 CFR 63.11132).
Determine whether the tanks are part of a stationary facility that dispenses gasoline into the fuel tanks of motor vehicles or nonroad engines (i.e., whether the facility functions as a GDF).

Confirm whether the tanks are used only to fuel company vehicles (on-site vehicle fueling) or are used to load/unload or redistribute gasoline to/from cargo tanks or other storage (on-site redistribution to other tanks).

Calculate the GDF monthly throughput: sum the volume of gasoline loaded into or dispensed from all gasoline storage tanks at the single GDF for the current day plus the previous 364 days, divided by 12, to determine whether throughput is <10,000 gal/month, ≥10,000 gal/month, or ≥100,000 gal/month (thresholds in 40 CFR 63.11111(b)–(d); definition reference 40 CFR 63.11132 'Monthly throughput').

Verify whether the tanks are located at a facility that is a bulk gasoline terminal, bulk gasoline plant, pipeline breakout station, or pipeline pumping station (if so, evaluate applicability under subpart BBBBBB).
Determine whether the item in question is a storage tank (covered by subpart CCCCCC) or equipment used for the refueling of motor vehicles (which 40 CFR 63.11112(a) states is not covered by CCCCCC).

If claiming the tanks are covered by subpart CCCCCC and throughput is below thresholds, ensure records documenting monthly throughput are available (records retention and demonstration requirements per 40 CFR 63.11111(e)).

For tanks that may be considered part of a bulk facility, verify whether they are used only for dispensing in a manner consistent with a GDF so that 40 CFR 63.11081(c) exclusion to subpart BBBBBB would apply.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Both key reasons in the EPA notes are present in the criteria: (1) the CCCCCC criteria state that stationary facilities that dispense gasoline into motor vehicle fuel tanks (GDFs) at area sources and the gasoline storage tanks at such GDFs are covered (captures EPA’s finding that the two gasoline tanks are subject to CCCCCC); and (2) the checklist/criteria require confirming fuel type and reference 40 CFR 63.11132 (including RVP) so diesel would be excluded as not being 'gasoline' (captures EPA’s reason that the diesel tank is not subject)."}

candidates.title: Portland cement plants (NESHAP Subpart LLL)

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a portland cement plant then inline coal mills associated with a kiln are affected sources under this subpart.

If there is an inline coal mill with a separate stack associated with a kiln then the combined PM emissions from the kiln and the inline coal mill stack (and alkali bypass, if any) are subject to the PM emissions limit in Table 1 of §63.1343(b).

If the coal mill exhaust is commingled with the kiln/clinker cooler/alkali bypass exhaust and routed as a single stream to the PM control device then the owner may meet an alternative (commingled) PM emission limit calculated using the equations in §63.1343(b)(2).

If the affected source is subject to PM limitations under §63.1343(b) then initial and subsequent PM performance tests must be conducted using EPA Method 5 or 5I and continuous performance must be demonstrated using a PM continuous parametric monitoring system (PM CPMS) as specified in §63.1349(b)(1) and §63.1350(b).

If the kiln exhaust is diverted through an alkali bypass or to a coal mill that exhausts through a separate stack then the main kiln exhaust and the alkali bypass and/or coal mill must be tested simultaneously and the combined PM emission rate computed for each test run as required for compliance testing.

If you need exhaust gas flow rates for an alkali bypass or coal mill stack for performance testing then you must either install, operate, calibrate and maintain a continuous exhaust gas flow instrument per the flow monitoring requirements or you may use the maximum design exhaust gas flow rate as allowed in §63.1349(a).

If you are using a PM CPMS to demonstrate continuous compliance then you must establish a site-specific operating limit from the performance test, repeat the PM performance test at least annually (or whenever instrument range or principal components change), and use the PM CPMS 30 kiln-operating-day rolling average to determine continuous compliance per §63.1349(b)(1) and §63.1350(b).

If the coal mill stack is used to account for other pollutants (THC, HCl, mercury) in calculating kiln-specific limits or combined emissions, then those pollutants must be measured either upstream of the coal mill or in the coal mill stack and accounted for in the flow-weighted calculations as specified in §63.1349 and the monitoring sections of §63.1350.

checklist: Confirm the facility is a portland cement plant and whether it is a major or area source (subject to Subpart LLL).
Confirm whether the coal mill is an inline coal mill associated with a specific kiln (i.e., listed as part of the kiln system) or a separate coal preparation source.
Confirm whether the coal mill exhaust is routed to its own separate stack or commingled with the kiln/clinker cooler/alkali bypass exhaust (single stream) prior to the PM control device.
If commingled, obtain Qk, Qc, Qab, and Qcm (exhaust flows in dscf/ton feed) and clinker production data needed to calculate the alternative PM limit using the equations in §63.1343(b)(2).
Identify the PM control device(s) serving the kiln and coal mill (e.g., baghouse or ESP) and the sampling locations for Method 5/5I testing.

Verify whether a continuous exhaust gas flow measurement instrument is installed and compliant with §63.1350(n) for the coal mill and alkali bypass stacks or whether the maximum design exhaust flow will be used for testing per §63.1349(a).

Determine whether a PM CPMS is installed or planned for the coal mill/kiln outlet, and collect instrument make/model, analytic principle, span/range and capability to meet the PM CPMS requirements in §63.1349(b)(1) and §63.1350(b).

Plan for simultaneous Method 5/5I performance testing of the kiln and the coal mill (and alkali bypass if present) and the calculation method (Equation 8 in §63.1349(b)(1)(viii)) to compute combined lb/ton clinker PM for each run.
Establish how clinker production (tons) will be measured/recorded (direct weigh scale or kiln feed with feed-to-clinker ratio) to meet §63.1350(d) requirements for lb/ton-clinker calculations.
Prepare to establish the PM CPMS site-specific operating limit from the initial Method 5/5I runs and to repeat the PM performance test annually or when instrument range/principal components change.

If also addressing THC, HCl, or mercury accounting, verify where those measurements will be taken (upstream of coal mill or in coal mill stack) and ensure monitoring systems meet the CEMS/CPMS requirements cited in §63.1349 and §63.1350.
Check whether the kiln burns hazardous waste (exclusion per §63.1340(b)(1)) which would change applicability (subject to subpart EEE instead).

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"OUR ANSWER captures the LLL requirements cited in the EPA NOTES (combined PM testing and annual/repeat PM testing per §§63.1349/63.1350), but it omits the EPA’s key point that the coal mill is also subject to NSPS Subpart Y (thermal dryer) — that dual applicability is not reflected in the criteria."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Secondary Aluminum Production

criteria.criterion: If a unit is used primarily to remove organic contaminants (for example oil, paint, lacquer, ink, plastic, or rubber) from aluminum scrap, then that unit meets the definition of a 'scrap dryer/delacquering kiln/decoating kiln' under this subpart.

If a scrap dryer/delacquering kiln/decoating kiln is located at a secondary aluminum production facility that is a major source of hazardous air pollutants (HAPs), then the requirements of this subpart apply to that unit (i.e., it is an affected source under Subpart RRR).

If a scrap dryer/delacquering kiln/decoating kiln is located at a secondary aluminum production facility that is an area source of HAPs, then the dioxin/furan (D/F) emission requirements and associated operating, monitoring, reporting, and recordkeeping requirements of this subpart apply to that unit.

If an establishment performs scrap drying/delacquering/decoating (even if it does not melt aluminum on-site), then that establishment meets the definition of a 'secondary aluminum production facility' for purposes of this subpart.
If the facility is used solely for research and development and is not used to produce a saleable product, then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to that facility or equipment.

If the site is an aluminum die casting facility, aluminum foundry, or aluminum extrusion facility and is an area source that does not emit (or have the potential to emit, considering controls) the major-source HAP thresholds, and the only regulated operation is a thermal chip dryer, then furnaces that melt only clean charge, internal scrap, or customer returns are not considered subject to this subpart.

checklist: Is the unit used primarily to remove organic contaminants (paint, lacquer, plastic, ink, oil, rubber) from aluminum scrap (i.e., does it function as a scrap dryer/delacquering kiln/decoating kiln)?

Does the facility perform any of the processes listed in the Subpart RRR definition of a secondary aluminum production facility (e.g., scrap shredding, scrap drying/delacquering/decoating, thermal chip drying, furnace operations, dross recovery)?
Is the facility a major source of HAPs (verify actual and potential emissions versus major-source thresholds) or an area source?
Are the delamination/delacquering units operated to produce a saleable product, or are they used only for research and development (no saleable product)?

Are you an aluminum die casting, foundry, or extrusion facility whose only potentially regulated operation is a thermal chip dryer and which otherwise melts only clean charge, internal scrap, or customer returns?
Do customers take the produced granules off-site and melt them (customer melts) or are the granules sold/used without melting (document intended use and any melting by customers)?

Record the process description and operating parameters of the delamination units (feedstock type, temperatures, residence time, whether an afterburner or control device is installed) to support classification under the definitions and applicability provisions.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Both key EPA reasons are captured: the criteria state the delamination chambers meet the 40 CFR 63.1503 definition of a scrap dryer/delacquering kiln/decoating kiln, and they explicitly note that performing delacquering/drying (even without on-site melting) brings the establishment within the secondary aluminum production definition (i.e., applicability no longer depends on whether the recovered aluminum is later melted)."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Paint Stripping and Miscellaneous Surface Coating Operations at Area Sources

criteria.criterion: If you operate an area source of HAP (not a major source) and you perform paint stripping using methylene chloride (MeCl), then you are subject to this subpart.

If you operate an area source of HAP and you perform spray application of coatings to motor vehicles and mobile equipment, then you are subject to this subpart unless you successfully demonstrate to the Administrator that you spray apply no coatings that contain the target HAP (or submit the May 9, 2023 notification in lieu of a petition).

If you operate an area source and you spray-apply coatings that contain the target HAP to plastic and/or metal substrates on parts or products (not motor vehicles/mobile equipment), then you are subject to this subpart.

If you operate an area source and you spray-apply no coatings that contain target HAP (as defined in § 63.11180) and you submit the required notification or petition demonstrating non-use of target HAP, then you may be exempted from the motor vehicle/mobile equipment surface coating provisions of this subpart, provided you retain required records and the Administrator does not disallow the exemption upon verification.

If you are an individual performing surface coating on personal vehicles or property as a hobby or for maintenance (or perform surface coating for others without compensation) and you do not exceed two motor vehicles or pieces of mobile equipment per year, then you are not subject to this subpart.

If your surface coating or paint stripping activities meet the definition of research and laboratory activities or of quality control activities, then those activities are not subject to this subpart.

If you perform paint stripping using MeCl, then you must implement the MeCl management practices and, if annual MeCl usage exceeds one ton, must develop and keep on-site a written MeCl minimization plan and maintain annual usage records on site.

If you are an affected motor vehicle/mobile equipment surface coating operation or miscellaneous surface coating operation, then you must meet the painter training, spray booth/enclosure and filter capture, approved spray equipment (transfer efficiency), and gun-cleaning practice requirements in § 63.11173(e) through (g).

If you are the owner or operator of a paint stripping operation using MeCl and/or a surface coating operation subject to this subpart, then you must submit the initial notification and, if applicable, the notification of compliance status as specified in § 63.11175.

checklist: Is your facility an area source of HAP (i.e., not a major source under 40 CFR 63.11170(b))?
Do you perform any paint stripping that uses methylene chloride (MeCl)?
What is your annual usage of MeCl (tons/year)? (If >1 ton/year, a written MeCl minimization plan is required and must be posted on-site.)
Do you perform spray application of coatings to motor vehicles or mobile equipment at a fixed location or as mobile repair/refinishing?

Do any of the coatings you spray-apply contain chromium, lead, manganese, nickel, or cadmium at or above the target HAP thresholds (use supplier formulation data/MSDS to verify concentrations per § 63.11180)?

Will you submit a May 9, 2023 notification to the Administrator (or petition) declaring you do not spray apply any target HAP-containing coatings? If so, where will you retain supporting records on-site?

Do any coating or stripping activities qualify as facility maintenance, research and laboratory activities, or quality control activities that would exempt them (see definitions in § 63.11180 and exclusions in § 63.11169(d))?
If you claim the hobby/personal-vehicle exception, how many motor vehicles/mobile equipment items do you spray-coat per year (does it exceed two)?
Are your painters certified and trained per the training requirements, and do you maintain a current list of personnel required to be trained?

Are spray booths/preparation stations/mobile enclosures equipped with filters demonstrated to achieve at least 98% capture of overspray and do booths meet enclosure and ventilation requirements in § 63.11173(e)(2)?
Are spray guns HVLP, electrostatic, airless, air-assisted airless, or demonstrated-equivalent transfer-efficiency equipment as required by § 63.11173(e)(3)?

Are spray gun cleaning practices performed so that atomized mist or spray of cleaning solvent/residue is not released outside a collecting container (e.g., enclosed gun washer) as required by § 63.11173(e)(4)?

Where are compliance records (initial notification, MeCl usage records, minimization plan, coating formulations/MSDS, training records, retention of exemption notification/petition) stored on-site and who is responsible for them?
Have you submitted (or do you need to submit) the initial notification and/or Notification of Compliance Status per § 63.11175, and do you have the information required by § 63.11175(a)(1)-(8) ready?

judge_text: {"score": 2, "reason": "All key reasons are present: the answer cites that MeCl paint stripping remains subject (63.11170(a)(1)/(b)); that spray-coating exemption hinges on demonstrating/no-use of target HAPs under 63.11170(a)(2) (and related notification/recordkeeping provisions); and that an initial notification/other compliance steps are required if target HAP coatings are ever used (63.11175)."}

candidates.title: Paint Stripping and Miscellaneous Surface Coating for Area Sources

criteria.criterion: If you operate an area source of HAP and perform paint stripping using methylene chloride (MeCl), then you are subject to this subpart.

If you operate an area source of HAP and perform spray application of coatings to motor vehicles and mobile equipment (except spray coating that meets the definition of facility maintenance), then you are subject to this subpart.

If you operate an area source of HAP and perform spray application of coatings that contain any of the target HAP (Cr, Pb, Mn, Ni, or Cd at the concentrations in the definition) to a plastic and/or metal substrate on a part or product (except facility maintenance or space vehicle), then you are subject to this subpart.
citations: 40 CFR 63.11180 (target HAP; target HAP containing coating)

criteria.criterion: If a specific spray-applied coating operation does not spray apply any target HAP-containing coatings (as defined in §63.11180), then that specific operation is not subject under §63.11170(a)(3).

If the source performs any activity listed in §63.11170(a), then the affected source (the collection of equipment listed in §63.11171(b)) is the entity subject to the subpart, which means other operations/equipment at the same affected source may be within the subpart's scope.

If you are the owner or operator of a motor vehicle or mobile equipment surface coating operation and you submit the required notification or petition certifying that you do not spray apply any target HAP-containing coatings, then you may be exempt from the motor vehicle/mobile equipment surface coating provisions (subject to Administrator verification).

checklist: Confirm that the facility is an area source (not a major source) per 40 CFR 63.11170(b) (i.e., verify that annual potential to emit is below 10 tpy for any single HAP and below 25 tpy combined).
Determine whether the polyurea line uses spray application as defined in §63.11180 (check equipment type and paint cup capacity; e.g., not non-atomizing methods or hand-held ≤3.0 fl oz exceptions).

Obtain and document formulation data/MSDS and calculate target HAP content of the polyurea coating as applied (use manufacturer formulation data and consider HAP content as applied, not just as purchased) to verify whether it contains chromium, lead, manganese, nickel, or cadmium at or above the thresholds in §63.11180.

Determine whether the parts coated on the polyurea line are motor vehicles or mobile equipment (or assembled motor vehicles) versus miscellaneous parts/products, because motor vehicle/mobile equipment provisions and petition/notification paths differ.
Verify whether the polyurea operation meets the definition of facility maintenance in §63.11180 (if so, it may be excluded).

Identify whether any other coating lines or operations at the same affected source spray-apply target HAP-containing coatings (because if any covered activity occurs at the affected source, the affected source as defined in §63.11171(b) may be subject and include the polyurea line).
Check whether the operation qualifies for any exclusions in §63.11169(d) (research and laboratory activities, quality control activities, activities covered under another area source NESHAP, etc.).

If the facility is a motor vehicle/mobile equipment surface coating operation and you intend to claim exemption, verify whether you have submitted the required notification or petition and retained the supporting records on-site as described in §63.11170(a)(2).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Yes — the answer includes the EPA's key rationale: the miscellaneous surface coating provisions apply only to operations that spray-apply target-HAP coatings, and a specific line that does not spray any target-HAP coating is not subject (cites §63.11170(a)(3) and §63.11180). It also captures the motor-vehicle/mobile-equipment distinction and notes the affected-source/other-lines caveat."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Stationary Combustion Turbines

criteria.criterion: If your unit is a new or reconstructed lean premix gas-fired stationary combustion turbine as defined by this subpart, then it must comply with the emission limitations and operating limitations in Table 1 and Table 2 of this subpart.

If your stationary combustion turbine is required to comply with the formaldehyde emission limitation and is not equipped with an oxidation catalyst, then you must petition the Administrator for operating limitations that you will monitor to demonstrate compliance, measure those parameters during the initial performance test, and continuously monitor them thereafter (unless you petition for approval of no additional operating limitations).

If you petition the Administrator for approval of additional operating limitations for a turbine without an oxidation catalyst, then the petition must include identification of the specific parameters proposed, a discussion of the relationship between those parameters and HAP emissions, how you will establish limit values, the measurement and monitoring methods and instruments (with accuracy/precision), and the frequency and methods for recalibrating the instruments.

If you petition the Administrator for approval of no additional operating limitations for a turbine without an oxidation catalyst, then the petition must include identification of parameters that could change, discussions of their relationship to HAP emissions, why limits are not possible or feasible, methods/instruments to measure and monitor them (with accuracy/precision), recalibration methods/frequency, and why adopting them is infeasible/unnecessary.

If you are operating a turbine that uses an oxidation catalyst to meet the formaldehyde limitation, then you must continuously monitor the catalyst inlet temperature to comply with the operating limitations referenced in Table 2 and Table 5 of this subpart.

If you are operating a turbine that is required to comply with the formaldehyde limitation and are not using an oxidation catalyst, then you must continuously monitor any parameters specified in your approved petition to the Administrator in order to comply with the operating limitations and monitoring requirements in this subpart.

If you are required to conduct the performance tests in Table 3 of this subpart, then you must conduct them according to that table, conduct three separate test runs each lasting at least one hour, and perform tests at high load defined as 100 percent plus or minus 10 percent (and for initial tests ensure representativeness and record supporting process information).

If your turbine is not equipped with an oxidation catalyst and you submit a petition under §63.6120, then you must not conduct the initial performance test until after the Administrator has approved or disapproved the petition.

If you are subject to this subpart and must conduct initial performance tests or other initial compliance demonstrations per Table 4, then you must do so within 180 calendar days after the compliance date specified for your turbine in §63.6095.

If you are required to comply with the formaldehyde emission limitation and conduct performance tests to demonstrate compliance, then you must submit a Notification of Compliance Status, including the performance test results, before the close of business on the 60th calendar day following completion of the performance test.

If you are required to use a continuous monitoring system (CMS) after September 8, 2020, then you must develop and implement a CMS quality control program with written procedures per this subpart and keep those procedures on record for the life of the affected source or until no longer subject to the part.

If your lean premix gas-fired or diffusion flame gas-fired turbine uses any quantity of distillate oil at the same major source, then you must monitor and record distillate oil usage daily with a non-resettable hour meter for all new and existing turbines at the major source.

If your turbine fires landfill gas, digester gas, or gasified MSW equal to 10 percent or more of gross heat input on an annual basis, then you must monitor and record fuel usage daily with separate fuel meters for each fuel and operate the turbine in a manner that minimizes HAP emissions.

checklist: Confirm the turbine type per subpart definitions: is it a lean premix gas-fired stationary combustion turbine?

Confirm whether the turbine is new or reconstructed and the exact start-up/installation date to determine applicable notification and compliance deadlines (e.g., initial notification within 120 days if started on/after March 5, 2004).
Confirm facility HAP source status (major vs. area source) and whether the turbine is subject to the formaldehyde emission limitation in this subpart.
Confirm whether the turbine is equipped with an oxidation catalyst (yes/no).

If no catalyst and you plan to rely on turbine speed and inlet air temperature, prepare a petition to the Administrator that: identifies those parameters; explains how changes in them affect formaldehyde/HAP emissions; proposes upper/lower limit values; describes measurement methods/instruments and their accuracy/precision; and specifies recalibration frequency and methods (per §63.6120(f)(1)-(5)).

If you plan instead to petition for no additional operating limitations, document the parameters that could change, explain relationship to HAPs, why limits are not feasible, potential measurement methods/instruments and recalibration (per §63.6120(g)(1)-(7)).

Do not schedule or conduct the initial performance test for outlet formaldehyde concentration until after the Administrator has approved or disapproved your petition (if you submitted one) per §63.6120(e).

Plan initial performance testing to meet subpart requirements: schedule within 180 days after your compliance date (§63.6110(a)), conduct three separate runs each ≥1 hour, at high load (100% ±10%), and record process information demonstrating representativeness (§63.6120(a),(c),(d)).

Prepare to submit required notifications: Initial Notification as applicable within 120 days (§63.6145(c)) and Notification of Compliance Status including performance test results within 60 days after test completion (§63.6145(f)).

If your petition is approved and specifies operating parameters, ensure continuous monitoring capability for the approved parameters and document monitoring methods, data recording, and instrument calibration procedures (per §63.6125(b) and §63.6120(f)(4)-(5)).
If you will use a CMS after September 8, 2020, develop and implement a CMS quality control program with written procedures and retain records per §63.6125(e).
If using an oxidation catalyst, ensure continuous catalyst inlet temperature monitoring is installed and documented per §63.6125(a).

If firing landfill/digester gas or gasified MSW ≥10% of gross heat input annually, install separate fuel meters and record daily fuel usage and document that operation minimizes HAP emissions per §63.6125(c).
If any distillate oil is fired in any turbine at the major source, install a non-resettable hour meter and record daily distillate oil usage for all turbines per §63.6125(d).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Yes — the answer cites §63.6120(e)-(f) requiring a petition for turbines without a catalyst, details the petition content (identify parameters, relationship to HAPs, limit values, monitoring methods, recalibration per §63.6120(f)), and cites §63.6125(b) requiring continuous monitoring of approved parameters, which together capture the EPA Notes (approval of %NGP and inlet air temperature as petitioned operating limits and requirement for continuous monitoring)."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Metal Fabrication and Finishing Area Sources (Metal Fabrication and Finishing Area Source NESHAP)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an area source that is primarily engaged (≥50% of production over the previous continuous 12 months) in operations in one of the nine metal fabrication and finishing source categories listed in § 63.11514(a)(1)–(9) then your facility is subject to this subpart.

If you use materials that contain or have the potential to emit metal fabrication and finishing HAP (MFHAP) as defined (cadmium, chromium, lead, nickel ≥0.1% by weight as metal; manganese ≥1.0% by weight as metal) then your affected source is subject to this subpart.

If your operations include dry abrasive blasting, machining, dry grinding/dry polishing with machines, spray-applied painting, or welding that use materials containing MFHAP or have the potential to emit MFHAP then the corresponding affected source(s) are subject to this subpart.

If the activities at the site are limited to tool or equipment repair operations, facility maintenance, or quality control activities as defined in this subpart then those activities are not subject to this subpart.

If the operations are performed on-site at installations owned or operated by the U.S. Armed Forces, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or the National Nuclear Security Administration then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If the operations produce military munitions (as defined in this subpart) manufactured by or for the U.S. Armed Forces, or use equipment directly and exclusively used to transport such munitions, then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If you perform dry abrasive blasting using materials that contain or have the potential to emit MFHAP in a vented enclosure then you must capture emissions and vent them to a filtration control device and meet the management practices in § 63.11516(a)(2); if blasting occurs in totally enclosed and unvented chambers or on objects >8 feet different management/monitoring requirements apply per § 63.11516(a)(1) and (a)(3).

If you perform spray-applied painting using paints that contain MFHAP then the spray painting affected source is subject to the spray painting standards (booth/room enclosure and filter efficiency, transfer efficiency methods, spray gun cleaning, worker training/certification, and recordkeeping) in § 63.11516(d).

If you perform welding operations using materials that contain or have the potential to emit MFHAP then the welding affected source is subject to the welding management practice requirements in § 63.11516(f), and if your welding affected source uses 2,000 pounds or more per year of welding rod containing MFHAP (rolling 12-month basis) then you must comply with the additional requirements and monitoring in § 63.11516(f)(3)–(8).

checklist: Confirm that your facility is an area source (verify area-source status per applicable EPA definition).

Determine whether your facility is "primarily engaged" (≥50% of production over the previous continuous 12 months) in one of the nine metal fabrication and finishing source categories in § 63.11514(a)(1)–(9) and document the production basis and calculation.

List all on-site operations (dry abrasive blasting, spray-applied painting, welding, machining, dry grinding/dry polishing with machines, etc.) and identify which operations occur regularly versus occasional maintenance.

Obtain formulation data/MSDS for all coatings, solvents, welding rods, and materials to determine MFHAP content (cadmium, chromium, lead, nickel ≥0.1% by weight; manganese ≥1.0% by weight) for each material used.

If abrasive blasting is performed, document whether blasting is in a totally enclosed and unvented chamber, a vented enclosure, or outdoors, and whether blasted objects exceed 8 feet in any dimension.
If abrasive blasting is vented, document capture and filtration control devices and retain manufacturer's specifications for the filtration control device.
If welding is conducted, calculate rolling 12-month usage of welding rod that contains MFHAP to determine if usage is ≥2,000 lb/year and retain records of the rolling 12-month calculation.

If spray painting is conducted with MFHAP-containing paints, document whether spray booths/rooms meet enclosure and filter efficiency requirements (98% capture per ASHRAE 52.1) or whether waterwash booths meet the alternative requirement, and document spray gun types (HVLP or equivalent) and worker training/certification records.
Determine whether the activities are classified as facility maintenance, tool/equipment repair, or quality control activities (per definitions) to assess possible exclusion.
Verify whether the site is owned/operated by the U.S. Armed Forces, NASA, or NNSA, or whether operations produce military munitions, which would exempt applicability.

As applicable, verify past compliance actions: whether initial notification and notification of compliance status were submitted by the deadlines and whether annual certification and compliance reports and required records are being maintained per § 63.11519.

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"The answer captures the core legal basis in the EPA notes that applicability depends on whether the facility is primarily engaged in one of the nine §63.11514(a) categories (and includes checklist steps to reassess prior fabricated-structural-metal classification and the repair/maintenance exclusion). However it does not reference or require checking EPA’s SIC/NAICS Q&A table or otherwise explicitly address EPA’s use of the SIC/NAICS code crosswalk cited in the Region 1 letter, so a key piece of the EPA reasoning is missing."}

candidates.title: Metal Fabrication and Finishing Area Source NESHAP (Subpart XXXXXX)

criteria.criterion: If the facility is an area source and is 'primarily engaged' (i.e., production of one or more products in one of the nine metal fabrication and finishing source categories represents at least 50 percent of facility production over the previous continuous 12 months), then the facility is subject to this subpart.

If the facility performs any of the affected-source activities defined in paragraphs (b)(1)–(5) (dry abrasive blasting, machining, dry grinding and dry polishing with machines, spray painting, or welding) using materials that contain MFHAP or that have the potential to emit MFHAP, then the corresponding affected-source provisions of this subpart apply to those operations.

If materials used at the facility contain MFHAP at or above the specified thresholds (cadmium, chromium, lead, or nickel ≥ 0.1 percent by weight as the metal; manganese ≥ 1.0 percent by weight as the metal) as shown by manufacturer/supplier formulation data or MSDS, then those materials are 'materials containing MFHAP' for applicability under this subpart.
If on-site operations are tool or equipment repair, facility maintenance, or quality control as defined in §63.11522, then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If construction or reconstruction of the affected source commenced before April 3, 2008 the affected source is an existing source, and if construction or reconstruction commenced on or after April 3, 2008 the affected source is a new source (which determines new vs existing source status under the subpart).

checklist: Confirm whether the facility is an 'area source' (i.e., total HAP emissions are below major source thresholds) versus a major source.

Assemble production records for the previous continuous 12 months and calculate the percentage of facility production (by volume, linear foot, square foot, or other appropriate metric) that is the manufacture/fabrication/forging of products described in Table 1 of this subpart; retain documentation supporting the calculation per §63.10(b)(3).

Identify which of the nine metal fabrication and finishing source categories in Table 1 best describes your products/operations (e.g., Fabricated Metal Products; Industrial Machinery and Equipment Finishing Operations; Valves and Pipe Fittings; etc.).

Count units (and production share) that undergo finishing processes (dry abrasive blasting, dry machining, dry grinding/polishing with machines, spray painting, welding) versus units that do not, for the prior 12 months.

Collect Material Safety Data Sheets / formulation data for all paints, welding rods/filler metals, base metals, abrasives and other materials to determine whether they contain MFHAP at or above the thresholds (cadmium, chromium, lead, nickel ≥0.1% by weight; manganese ≥1.0% by weight).

Determine whether on-site finishing activities are production (fabrication/finishing of products for sale) or are facility maintenance, tool/equipment repair, or quality control (compare operations to definitions in §63.11522).
For abrasive blasting: determine whether blasting is dry or wet, whether blasting is performed in totally enclosed/unvented chambers or vented enclosures, and whether blast media contain MFHAP.

For machining and dry grinding/polishing: confirm whether operations are 'dry' (no lubricating fluids) and whether captured emissions are vented to filtration control devices (and keep manufacturer specifications for control devices).

For spray painting: determine whether paints are spray-applied as defined, whether paints contain MFHAP, whether spray booths/rooms or waterwash booths are used, and whether filters meet the 98% capture demonstration (retain vendor data or test results) and worker training/certification records per the schedule.

For welding: determine if welding rods used contain MFHAP and total annual usage of such welding rods (pounds per rolling 12-month period) to check the 2,000 lb/yr threshold for additional welding requirements; inventory capture/control equipment and manufacturer specs.
Gather records of any existing emission capture/control devices and their manufacturer's operation specifications (to demonstrate operation per manufacturer's instructions where required).

Document and retain the rationale and supporting records for the 'primarily engaged' determination and any determinations that operations are exempt (facility maintenance, tool repair, quality control) as required by §63.10(b)(3).

judge_text: {"score": 1, "reason": "The answer includes the correct subpart, identifies pumps as falling in the Industrial Machinery and Equipment Finishing Operations category, and cites the ‘primarily engaged’ 50% production test (40 CFR 63.11514/63.11522). However, the checklist also instructs counting the share of units that undergo finishing (dry blasting, painting, etc.), which contradicts the EPA note that ‘primarily engaged’ is based on production of the listed products (pumps) regardless of what fraction receive finishing. Thus some but not all key EPA reasons are captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Stationary Reciprocating Internal Combustion Engines

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a stationary RICE located at a major or area source of HAP emissions then that engine is an affected source potentially subject to this subpart.

If the engine is a non-road engine as defined at 40 CFR 1068.30 or is used to propel a motor vehicle or a vehicle used solely for competition then it is not a stationary RICE and is not subject to this subpart.
If the engine meets the definition of an emergency stationary RICE (including meeting the operating provisions in § 63.6640(f)) then that engine is not subject to this subpart.

If the stationary RICE is new or reconstructed and located at an area source then you must meet the requirements of 40 CFR part 60 subpart IIII (for compression ignition engines) or subpart JJJJ (for spark ignition engines) and no further requirements apply under this part for such engines.

If the engine is an existing stationary RICE located at an area source then you must comply with the emission limitations in Table 2d and the operating limitations in Table 2b of this subpart that apply to your engine.

If the engine's classification as existing, new, or reconstructed depends on its site-rated brake HP and the dates construction or reconstruction commenced, then apply the thresholds and date cutoffs in § 63.6590(1)-(3) to determine which provisions apply.

checklist: Determine whether each diesel engine is a 'stationary RICE' (not a non-road engine under 40 CFR 1068.30 and not used to propel a motor vehicle); document whether engines are considered mobile/nonroad or remain stationary when in use.
Document how each engine is mounted/installed on the portable vacuum unit and whether that mounting makes the engine a non-road/mobile engine under 40 CFR 1068.30.
Confirm fuel and engine type (diesel = compression ignition) for each engine to identify applicability of CI engine provisions or 40 CFR part 60 subpart IIII.
Measure or record the site-rated brake horsepower (HP) for each engine.
Record construction or reconstruction start dates for each engine to classify as existing, new, or reconstructed per § 63.6590 date thresholds.
Calculate facility-wide potential to emit (PTE) of HAPs (including beryllium): is any single HAP ≥ 10 tons/year or combined HAPs ≥ 25 tons/year (major) or below those thresholds (area)?
If claiming the engine is an emergency engine, document how and when it is used and verify it meets the emergency stationary RICE definition and the operating requirements in § 63.6640(f).
Verify whether any engine is being tested at a stationary RICE test cell/stand (engines being tested at a test cell/stand are excluded).

If any engine is new or reconstructed and at an area source, verify applicability of 40 CFR part 60 subpart IIII (CI) or JJJJ (SI) and prepare to comply with those subpart requirements in lieu of further Part 63 requirements.

For existing area-source engines, identify and review the specific requirements and management practices in Table 2d and operating limitations in Table 2b of Subpart ZZZZ that would apply to your engine(s).
Retain records supporting all determinations (stationary vs non-road, HP, build/commencement dates, PTE calculations, emergency-use documentation, and any § 63.6640(f) compliance).

judge_text: {"score": 1, "reason": "The answer captures the core basis in the EPA notes that engines meeting the nonroad definition in 40 CFR 1068.30 are not stationary RICE (criterion and checklist items reference nonroad/mobile status), but it fails to explicitly capture the 12-consecutive-months/site residency condition that EPA cited as the limiting factor for portable/transportable units (the checklist asks to document whether engines 'remain stationary' but does not state the 12-month rule)." }

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Engine Test Cells/Stands (Engine Test Cells/Stands NESHAP)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an engine test cell/stand that is located at a major source of HAP emissions, then you are subject to this subpart.
If the apparatus is used for testing uninstalled stationary or uninstalled mobile (motive) engines, then it meets the definition of an engine test cell/stand for this subpart.
If an engine is not installed in, or an integrated part of, the final product, then it is an uninstalled engine under this subpart.

If the plant site emits or has the potential to emit a single HAP at a rate of 10 tons per year or more, or any combination of HAP at a rate of 25 tons per year or more, then the site is a major source for purposes of this subpart.

If the affected source is an existing affected source (construction or reconstruction commenced on or before May 14, 2002), then existing affected sources do not have to meet the requirements of this subpart and of subpart A.

If any portion of a new or reconstructed affected source located at a major source is used exclusively for testing internal combustion engines with rated power less than 25 horsepower, then that portion does not have to meet this subpart's requirements (except initial notification in § 63.9345(b)).

If any portion of a new or reconstructed affected source is used exclusively for testing combustion turbine engines, rocket engines, research/teaching activities not for commercial engine development/test services, or for testing/evaluating fuels, transmissions, or electronics, then that portion does not have to meet this subpart's requirements.

If you have a new or reconstructed affected source used in whole or in part for testing internal combustion engines with rated power of 25 hp or more at a major source, then you must comply with the emission limitations in Table 1 to this subpart.

checklist: Is the apparatus used to test the diesel truck engines described an 'engine test cell/stand' (i.e., used for testing uninstalled stationary or uninstalled mobile engines)? (40 CFR 63.9285(a), 63.9375)
Are the diesel truck engines 'uninstalled' (not installed in or integrated into the final product)? (40 CFR 63.9285(b), 63.9375)

Is the plant site a major source of HAPs (single HAP ≥ 10 tpy or total HAPs ≥ 25 tpy) based on actual or potential to emit calculations and any federally enforceable limits? (40 CFR 63.9285(c), 63.9375)
Was construction or reconstruction of the affected source commenced on or before May 14, 2002 (i.e., is the affected source an 'existing affected source')? (40 CFR 63.9290(a)(1), 63.9290(b))
Are the engines' rated power values ≥ 25 horsepower, or is any portion used exclusively for testing engines < 25 hp? (40 CFR 63.9290(c), 63.9300)

Is any portion of the affected source used exclusively for testing combustion turbine engines, rocket engines, or for research/teaching not engaged in commercial engine development/test services? (40 CFR 63.9290(d)(1)-(3))

Is any portion of the affected source operated to test or evaluate fuels, transmissions, or electronics (including clutch testing classified as transmission testing) and, if so, is that portion used exclusively for such testing? (40 CFR 63.9290(d)(4))

If the source appears to be a new or reconstructed affected source at a major source and tests engines ≥ 25 hp, verify the applicable emission limitation Table 1 requirements and initial notification applicability (Table 1 reference and 63.9345(b)). (40 CFR 63.9300, 63.9290(c))

judge_text: {"score": 1, "reason": "Some EPA reasons are reflected (the answer includes the definition that the subpart covers apparatus used to test uninstalled engines—i.e., engines being tested—and lists exclusions for specific testing activities). However the EPA notes’ two key points are missing: (1) the 12‑month/temporary threshold that engines kept in test cells beyond 12 months are treated as stationary RICE (not captured in the criteria), and (2) the explicit exclusion that the engine‑test‑cell exception does NOT apply where the engine is used merely as a power source to test other components (e.g., clutches)—the answer instead treats clutch/transmission testing as a possible exempt category without the EPA’s limiting clarification."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Coal- and Oil-Fired Electric Utility Steam Generating Units

criteria.criterion: if you own or operate a coal-fired EGU or an oil-fired EGU as defined in § 63.10042 then you are subject to this subpart

if the unit is an electric utility steam generating unit that is not a coal- or oil-fired EGU and meets the definition of a natural gas-fired EGU in § 63.10042 then the unit is not subject to this subpart

if the unit is a 'fossil fuel-fired' EGU (i.e., capable of producing >25 MWe and having fuels allowed in its operating permit and appropriate fuel handling facilities) and burns oil for more than 10.0 percent of the average annual heat input during the 3 previous calendar years or more than 15.0 percent of the annual heat input during any one of those calendar years then it is an oil-fired EGU and subject to this subpart

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Major Sources: Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers and Process Heaters

criteria.criterion: if you own or operate an industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler or process heater located at, or part of, a major source of HAP then the unit is subject to this subpart except as specified in § 63.7491

if the unit is an electric utility steam generating unit covered by subpart UUUUU or is a natural gas-fired EGU firing at least 85 percent natural gas on an annual heat input basis then the unit is not subject to this subpart

checklist: Is the unit an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) that serves a generator producing electricity for sale (document gross/net electrical output and whether >25 MWe)?
Does the unit have the capability to combust fossil fuels (are fuels allowed in the operating permit and are fuel handling facilities for coal or oil present)?

Calculate percent heat input from oil: the 3‑calendar‑year rolling average oil heat input (%) and the oil heat input (%) in each of those individual years (compare to >10% 3‑yr avg or >15% any one year per 40 CFR 63.10042)

Calculate percent heat input from natural gas: the 3‑calendar‑year rolling average natural gas heat input (%) and current-year natural gas heat input (%) and whether annual natural gas heat input is ≥85% (for exclusion from subpart DDDDD per 40 CFR 63.7491(a))

If oil is used, determine oil type (liquid distillate/residual oil versus solid oil‑derived fuel) and whether the unit might qualify as a limited‑use liquid oil‑fired unit (annual capacity factor when burning oil <8% averaged over a 24‑month contiguous period) per definitions in 40 CFR 63.10042
Is the facility a major source of HAP (major source status for applicability to subpart DDDDD)?

Is the unit physically and administratively treated as an EGU (e.g., sells electricity to the grid, cogeneration status and fraction of useful thermal/electric output) per the EGU definitions in 40 CFR 63.10042

Verify whether the unit was projected to meet fuel‑use thresholds for the first three years after the compliance date (owners/operators are responsible for estimates per 40 CFR 63.10042) and maintain documentation of those projections and actual fuel use records

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Both key EPA reasons are represented: the UUUUU criteria and checklist capture the oil fuel thresholds (3‑yr >10% or any year >15%) so the unit would not be an oil‑fired EGU under §63.10042, and the DDDDD criteria cite §63.7491(a)/§63.10042 and the ≥85% natural‑gas check that exclude a natural gas‑fired EGU from subpart DDDDD."}

candidates.title: Pesticide active ingredient (PAI) process units (Subpart MMM)

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a major source and the facility-wide collection of pesticide active ingredient manufacturing process units (PAI process units) process, use, or produce HAP at the plant site, then the affected source is subject to this subpart.
