If construction or reconstruction of an affected source commenced after November 10, 1997, or a dedicated PAI process unit commenced construction after November 10, 1997 (or reconstruction after September 20, 2002) and the dedicated unit has the potential to emit ≥10 tons/yr of any one HAP or ≥25 tons/yr of combined HAP, then the source (or dedicated unit) is a new affected source subject to the new-source requirements of this subpart.
If a PAI process unit is subject to another subpart of 40 CFR part 63 (e.g., is an affected source under that other subpart), then that PAI process unit is not subject to Subpart MMM.

If a storage vessel’s input to the vessel from the PAI process unit is greater than or equal to the input from any other PAI or non-PAI process unit or the vessel’s output to the PAI process unit is greater than or equal to the output to any other PAI or non-PAI process unit, then that storage vessel is part of the affected source subject to this subpart.
If equipment is intended to operate in organic HAP service for less than 300 hours during the calendar year, then that equipment is exempt from the requirements of this subpart.

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing Process Units (MCPU) (Subpart FFFF)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) that are located at, or are part of, a major source of HAP, then you are subject to the requirements of this subpart.

If an MCPU produces materials described by the cited SIC/NAICS classifications (or the specific materials listed such as quaternary ammonium compounds, hydrazine, or nondedicated solvent recovery) and the MCPU processes, uses, or generates any organic HAP or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP, then the equipment meets the MCPU definition and may be subject to this subpart.

If the MCPU is an affected source or part of an affected source under another subpart of 40 CFR part 63 (except for certain batch process vent situations noted in §63.100), then subpart FFFF does not apply to that MCPU (i.e., it is not an affected source under FFFF).
If the operation is one of the exclusions listed (for example a research and development facility or other items in paragraph (c)), then the requirements of this subpart do not apply.

If construction or reconstruction of the affected source commenced after April 4, 2002 and the applicability criteria were met at that time, or if a dedicated MCPU commenced construction after April 4, 2002 and has the potential to emit ≥10 tpy of any one HAP or ≥25 tpy of combined HAP, then the source or dedicated MCPU is a new affected source under this subpart.

checklist: Is the plant a major source of HAP under CAA section 112(a) (total facility HAP emissions in tpy)?

Is the distillation column being added part of a PAI process unit (i.e., used to produce the pesticide active ingredient 2,4‑D or an integral intermediate for it) as defined in 40 CFR 63.1361 (determine primary product use and whether >50% of intermediate is used on‑site)?

Are the existing tanks that hold the purchased raw material assigned to the PAI process unit under the input/output rules (is the input from or output to the PAI process unit ≥ input/output to any other process) or is there an intervening storage vessel or separate building that would change assignment?

What are the construction/reconstruction start dates for the new distillation column and related equipment (compare to Nov 10, 1997 and Apr 4, 2002) to determine new vs existing source status under the subparts?
What is the potential to emit (PTE) for the distillation unit and associated vents/controls in tpy for each individual HAP and for combined HAP (is any ≥10 tpy or combined ≥25 tpy)?
Does the distillation process or raw material process, use, or generate any organic HAP or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP and at what concentrations (to determine MCPU and PAI applicability)?
Is the operation (or any portion) already subject to another 40 CFR part 63 subpart (e.g., PAI/other MACT) such that subpart FFFF would not apply?
Will any equipment be operated in organic HAP service for less than 300 hours/year (potential exemption under MMM)?

Are the storage vessel characteristics relevant (capacity, maximum true vapor pressure, and whether vapor balancing or controls will be used) to determine Group 1/Group 2 storage vessel status under Subpart MMM?
If considering Subpart FFFF, does the process fall within the listed SIC/NAICS product categories or other specific material groups in §63.2435(b)(1) (document NAICS/SIC and product description)?

candidates.title: Definitions for the chemical preparations area source rule

criteria.criterion: If the operation is a chemical preparation operation used to manufacture chemical preparations (under NAICS 325998) that manufactures target HAP-containing products or intermediates (where target HAP includes nickel at or above the target thresholds), then the equipment and materials meet the definitions used by this subpart and may fall within its scope.
If equipment in the chemical preparation operation contains, contacts, or is processing target HAP-containing materials, then that equipment is considered to be 'in target HAP service'.

If the cathode mixing uses mixing and blending equipment (including mixing of wet or dry materials) to manufacture chemical preparations as defined, then those activities meet the subpart's definition of a chemical preparations operation.

candidates.title: Paints and allied products area source standards

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a facility that performs paints and allied products manufacturing that is an area source and processes, uses, or generates materials containing HAP, then you are subject to this subpart.

If you add dry pigments or solids that contain nickel to a process vessel or to a grinding/milling process, then you must capture particulate emissions during the addition and route them to a particulate control device (or comply with the alternative compliance options specified).

If pigments and other solids that contain nickel are added to the process only in paste, slurry, or liquid form, then the requirement to capture particulate emissions during addition does not apply for those additions.
If the facility is a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7), then it is not subject to this subpart.

candidates.title: Chemical manufacturing area source (CMPU) applicability

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a chemical manufacturing process unit (CMPU) located at an area source and the CMPU uses as feedstock any material that contains any Table 1 HAP at an individual concentration greater than 0.1 percent by weight (or specific higher thresholds for quinoline, manganese, or trivalent chromium), then this subpart applies to that CMPU.

If the cathode mixing and associated vessels, transfer operations, and surge receivers are part of a process that falls within NAICS code 325 (chemical manufacturing), then they are included in the CMPU definition for this subpart.
If the operations are subject to the paints and allied products area source standards (subpart CCCCCCC), then this chemical manufacturing subpart does not apply to those operations.

checklist: Determine the facility NAICS code(s) that cover the cathode slurry mixing (e.g., whether the activity is classified under NAICS 325, NAICS 325998, or under paints & allied products NAICS).
Confirm whether the battery cell plant will be an area source (vs major source) of HAP emissions.

Obtain formulation data or SDS for the nickel-containing active material and any other feedstocks to determine nickel (and other Table 1 HAP) concentrations by weight in the raw materials (use upper bound if SDS presents a range).
Determine whether the nickel-containing material meets the 'target HAP-containing' threshold (nickel compounds ≥ 0.1% by weight) referenced in the chemical preparations definitions.
Determine the physical form of the nickel-containing material at the point of addition: added as a dry powder/solid, or already in paste/slurry/liquid form.
Determine whether the cathode mixing equipment and activities are considered a 'chemical preparation operation' (mixing, blending, milling, extruding) as defined in 40 CFR 63.11588.
If materials containing Table 1 HAP are present, confirm whether the cathode mixing and associated vessels, transfers, and surge receivers form a CMPU at the facility.

Check whether the facility or the specific mixing operations are instead part of paints and allied products manufacturing (which would make subpart CCCCCCC the applicable area source rule and exclude VVVVVV per §63.11494(c)(1)(i)).
Confirm whether the operation qualifies as research and development (R&D) excluded from the paints subpart per §63.11599(e), if claiming that status.

If dry nickel-containing powders are added, document whether capture and particulate control will be used (per the paints subpart requirements) or whether additions are exclusively in slurry/paste form to evaluate the exemptions in §63.11601.

The answer captures that nickel is a HAP (check Table 1/target HAP thresholds) and that if operations are subject to the paints & allied products area source rule then the CMPU rule is excluded (§63.11494(c)(1)(i)). However the answer does not explicitly capture the EPA’s central classification rationale that the cathode slurry is a coating that leaves a dried film (i.e., fits the paints/coatings definition under the paints subpart, cited by EPA at §63.11607), nor does it cite §63.11607 directly. Therefore only some EPA key reasons are reflected."}

candidates.title: Area source standards for glass manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a plant site that manufactures flat glass, glass containers, or pressed and blown glass by melting a mixture of raw materials to produce molten glass and form the molten glass into sheets, containers, or other shapes, then the site meets the definition of a glass manufacturing facility for this subpart and could be subject.

If your plant is an area source of HAP emissions (PTE < 9.07 Mg/yr [10 tpy] for any single HAP and < 22.68 Mg/yr [25 tpy] for combined HAP), then it meets the area-source status requirement of this subpart.

If your glass manufacturing facility uses one or more continuous furnaces to produce glass that contains compounds of one or more glass manufacturing metal HAP as raw materials, then the facility meets the process/materials criterion for this subpart.

If a specific glass melting furnace is (1) a continuous furnace, (2) charged with compounds of one or more glass manufacturing metal HAP as raw materials, and (3) used to produce glass at a rate of at least 45 Mg/yr (50 tpy), then that furnace is an affected glass melting furnace under this subpart.
If a furnace is a research and development process unit as defined in the subpart, then that furnace is not an affected furnace under this subpart.
If you own or operate an area source that is subject to this subpart, then you must obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or 40 CFR part 71.

candidates.title: Area source standards for paints and allied products manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a facility that performs paints and allied products manufacturing that is an area source of HAP emissions and the facility processes, uses, or generates materials containing HAP, then the facility is subject to this subpart.
If a facility no longer processes, uses, or generates materials containing HAP and does not plan to do so in the future, then the facility is no longer subject to this subpart.
If the facility is a research and development facility as defined in section 112(c)(7) of the Clean Air Act, then the standards of this subpart do not apply.

If you are exempt from the obligation to obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or 71 (subject to the stated conditions), then you remain required to comply with the provisions of this subpart even if you do not hold a title V permit.

candidates.title: Area source standards for chemical preparations

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a chemical preparations facility that is a stationary area source of HAP and the facility has at least one chemical preparations operation in target HAP service, then the facility (all chemical preparations operations) is subject to this subpart.

If your chemical preparations operations at your facility are subject to the requirements specified in subpart VVVVVV or subpart CCCCCCC of this part, then you are exempt from the requirements of this subpart.

If your chemical preparations operation becomes a major source on or after December 30, 2009, then you must continue to meet the requirements of this subpart in addition to any MACT standards that may apply.
If the facility is a research and development facility as defined in section 112(c)(7) of the Clean Air Act, then this subpart does not apply.
If you are exempt from the obligation to obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or 71 (subject to the stated conditions), then you still must continuously comply with the provisions of this subpart.

checklist: Does the plant melt raw materials to produce molten glass and form the molten glass into sheets, containers, or other shapes (does frit production involve producing molten glass and forming/quenching it into a glass product)? (see 40 CFR 63.11448(a))
Is the facility an area source of HAPs (potential-to-emit < 9.07 Mg/yr [10 tpy] for any single HAP and < 22.68 Mg/yr [25 tpy] for combined HAP)? (see 40 CFR 63.11448(b))

Are the furnaces used in your process continuous furnaces as defined by the glass subpart, and are they charged with compounds of one or more glass manufacturing metal HAP (for example, nickel compounds)? (see 40 CFR 63.11448(c) and 40 CFR 63.11449(a)(1)-(2))
What is the annual production rate of glass (or frit) from each furnace in Mg/yr and tpy; is any furnace producing glass at ≥45 Mg/yr (50 tpy)? (see 40 CFR 63.11449(a)(3))
Is any furnace at the facility a research and development process unit (R&D) as defined in the relevant subpart definitions? (see 40 CFR 63.11449(b))
Does the facility perform paints and allied products manufacturing operations, and does it process, use, or generate materials containing HAP in those operations? (see 40 CFR 63.11599(a)-(b))
Does the facility qualify as a chemical preparations facility and does it have at least one chemical preparations operation in target HAP service? (see 40 CFR 63.11579(a))
Are any chemical preparations operations at the facility already subject to subpart CCCCCCC (paints) or subpart VVVVVV, which would exempt them from subpart BBBBBBB? (see 40 CFR 63.11579(f))
Has any chemical preparations operation at the facility become a major source on or after December 30, 2009? (see 40 CFR 63.11579(c))
Is the facility a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7), which would exempt it from these area source subparts? (see 40 CFR 63.11599(e) and 40 CFR 63.11579(d))

Are you required to obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or part 71 (or otherwise required under 40 CFR 70.3(a) or 71.3(a))? (relevant to permit obligations referenced in 40 CFR 63.11449(e), 40 CFR 63.11599(c), and 40 CFR 63.11579(e))

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Secondary Aluminum Production

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a secondary aluminum production facility as defined in §63.1503 and is a major source of hazardous air pollutants (HAPs), then each thermal chip dryer at the facility is an affected source subject to this subpart.

If the facility is an area source of HAPs (not a major source), then the dioxin/furan (D/F) requirements and associated operating, monitoring, reporting, and recordkeeping requirements of this subpart apply to each thermal chip dryer at the facility.

If the unit is used solely to remove water from aluminum scrap (for example, a pre-heating box or other dryer used solely for water removal), then it is not considered a thermal chip dryer for purposes of this subpart and is not an affected source under this subpart.

If the device meets the subpart's definition of a thermal chip dryer (a device that uses heat to evaporate oil or oil/water mixtures from unpainted/uncoated aluminum chips), then it is an affected source listed in §63.1500(b)(2) and is subject to the thermal chip dryer emission limits (THC and D/F) in §63.1505(c).

If the thermal chip dryer is equipped with an afterburner (or other control device) to meet subpart requirements, then afterburner-specific performance test and continuous monitoring requirements apply (including establishing operating parameter values and continuous afterburner temperature monitoring and recording).

If a performance test is required for the thermal chip dryer, then the owner/operator must conduct a performance test measuring THC and D/F emissions at the outlet of the control device while the unit processes only unpainted aluminum chips.

checklist: Confirm that your facility qualifies as a "secondary aluminum production facility" per 40 CFR 63.1503 (i.e., performs scrap shredding, scrap drying/delacquering/decoating, thermal chip drying, furnace operations, dross recovery, in-line fluxing, or dross cooling).

Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAPs (potential to emit thresholds per 40 CFR 63.2) or an area source, because applicability and which provisions apply differ for major vs. area sources.
Verify whether the dryer will be used solely to remove water from scrap (pre-heating/water-only dryers) — if yes, it is not a thermal chip dryer under this subpart.

Verify the material charged to the unit: are they unpainted/uncoated aluminum chips, or shredded scrap that contains paint/coatings? (the thermal chip dryer definition refers to unpainted/uncoated chips and performance tests are run while processing only unpainted chips).

Record the intended operating temperature of the dryer (your ~660 °F), since 40 CFR 63.1503 notes scrap dried at ≥343 °C (650 °F) is identified in the definition of 'clean charge' (this affects charge classification and downstream furnace status).

Confirm whether the dryer will be equipped with an afterburner or other add-on control device; if so, prepare for afterburner performance test and continuous temperature monitoring and recording per the subpart.

Plan for feed/charge weight or aluminum production measurement capability (accuracy ±1%) for emission rate calculations if subject to kg/Mg (lb/ton) or µg/Mg limits (see monitoring and test requirements).

If you will perform a performance test, confirm you can run the test while processing only unpainted aluminum chips (as required for the thermal chip dryer test) and that test/monitoring protocols (THC, D/F) can be met.

If the facility is an aluminum die casting, aluminum foundry, or aluminum extrusion facility, verify whether the facility meets the limited-area-source conditional definition in 40 CFR 63.1500(f) (this can affect which units at the facility are subject).

The answer includes major vs area source applicability, the water-only (preheat) exception, and asks whether the material is painted scrap (so it partly covers why a painted-scrap dryer would be regulated). However it does not explicitly state that drying painted shreds is a 'scrap dryer/delacquering/decoating kiln' under §63.1503 (the specific basis EPA cited) and it fails to capture EPA’s key point that operating at ~660 °F does not demonstrate absence of HAP emissions and therefore does not exempt the unit from the standard."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Electric Utility Steam Generating Units (EGUs) (MATS)

criteria.criterion: If the unit meets the definition of an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) in § 63.10042 and is not listed as excluded in § 63.9983, then the unit is subject to subpart UUUUU emission limits (except during periods of startup or shutdown).

If the EGU is coal-fired, liquid oil-fired, or solid oil-derived fuel-fired, then during periods of startup or shutdown you must meet the work practice requirements in Table 3 to this subpart rather than the numeric emission limits for those periods.

If you apply the current definition of 'startup' in paragraph (1) of § 63.10042 (the post‑January 2, 2025 definition), then a firing after a shutdown for any purpose (including to produce auxiliary steam for on-site use) is considered startup only until the steam is first used for any purpose (including on-site use), and startup ends at that moment (after which the normal emission limits apply).

If you elect to rely on paragraph (2) of the definition of 'startup' in § 63.10042 (only allowed prior to January 2, 2025 pursuant to § 63.10000(m)), then firing after a shutdown to make useful thermal energy (for example auxiliary steam) may qualify as startup and that startup period ends 4 hours after the EGU makes useful thermal energy or 4 hours after it generates electricity sold or used, whichever is earlier, and the additional monitoring and reporting requirements in § 63.10020(e) apply if you rely on paragraph (2).

checklist: Is the unit an 'electric utility steam generating unit (EGU)' per 40 CFR 63.10042 (e.g., >25 MWe, serves a generator that produces electricity for sale, and meets the fuel-type/fraction tests)?
Is the unit excluded under any paragraph of 40 CFR 63.9983 (for example, a natural gas‑fired EGU that meets the subpart's natural gas definition or other listed exclusions)?
What fuel(s) does the unit burn, and do coal or oil heat‑input fractions meet the thresholds in 40 CFR 63.10042 to classify it as coal‑fired or oil‑fired (average annual heat input over prior years)?
Is the unit a limited‑use liquid oil‑fired EGU (meeting the <8% oil capacity factor definition) which changes applicability of emission limits vs work practices?
Was the firing to produce auxiliary steam initiated after a shutdown event (i.e., does the event meet the trigger for 'startup' under § 63.10042)?
For the particular auxiliary‑steam‑only operation: is the steam being used on‑site (e.g., to heat fuel tanks) or sold/used off‑site (i.e., when is steam 'used' per the definition)?
What definition of 'startup' will you rely on (paragraph (1) effective after Jan 2, 2025, or paragraph (2) if you previously elected it before Jan 2, 2025)?
How long will the auxiliary‑steam operation last (to determine whether a 4‑hour startup window under paragraph (2) would apply if elected)?

Have you implemented the Table 3 work practices and the required monitoring, data collection, and reporting for startup/shutdown periods (including site‑specific monitoring plan, CMS/sorbent trap set up, and the hourly records required by § 63.10020(e) if relying on paragraph (2))?

Do your monitoring systems (CMS, PM CPMS, sorbent traps, etc.) collect and record data during the auxiliary‑steam operation and are you prepared to treat that period as either 'startup' or normal operation in your emissions averaging and reports per §§ 63.10020–63.10021?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's key point—that under §63.10042(1) startup ends when steam is generated/used for any purpose (including on‑site auxiliary steam), so producing auxiliary steam is not startup—is explicitly included in OUR ANSWER (criterion citing §63.10042(1)) and reinforced in the checklist; the alternative paragraph (2) election and its 4‑hour rule are also captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Coal- and Oil-Fired Electric Utility Steam Generating Units (EGUs)

criteria.criterion: if the unit is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) — i.e., a fossil fuel-fired combustion unit capable of producing more than 25 megawatts electric that serves a generator that produces electricity for sale — then the unit is potentially subject to subpart UUUUU

if the unit burns oil for more than 10 percent of the average annual heat input during the 3 previous calendar years (or more than 15 percent during any one of those years), then the unit meets the definition of an oil-fired EGU and is in the oil-fired subcategory considered by this subpart

if the unit's annual capacity factor for oil (calculated as total annual heat input from oil divided by maximum hourly heat input regardless of fuel multiplied by 8,760 hours) is less than 8 percent averaged over a 24-month contiguous period commencing on the first of the month following the compliance date specified in § 63.9984, then the unit qualifies as a limited-use liquid oil-fired EGU and is not subject to the numeric emission limits in Tables 1 and 2 but must comply with the tune-up work practice requirements in Table 3

if the unit is capable of combusting more than 25 MW of coal or oil but did not fire sufficient oil to meet the oil-fired EGU definition (i.e., did not meet the >10%/>15% oil thresholds), then the unit is not subject to this subpart

if the unit meets the definition of a natural gas-fired EGU under this subpart (i.e., does not meet the oil- or coal-fired EGU thresholds for recent years), then the unit is not subject to this subpart

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers and Process Heaters (Boiler MACT)

criteria.criterion: if the boiler is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) covered by subpart UUUUU, then the boiler is not subject to subpart DDDDD
if the unit is a natural gas-fired EGU firing at least 85 percent natural gas on an annual heat input basis, then the unit is not subject to subpart DDDDD

checklist: Confirm whether Unit 1 serves a generator and produces electricity for sale (i.e., determine EGUs status).
Confirm the unit's maximum hourly heat input (nameplate or permitted MMBtu/hr) and maximum sustainable electrical output (MW) as applicable.

Compile annual heat input by fuel type (MMBtu/year) for the relevant recent years (at least the previous 3 calendar years and the most recent 24-month contiguous period) showing heat input from No. 2 and No. 4 fuel oil and from natural gas.
Calculate the percent of annual heat input provided by oil for each of the previous 3 calendar years and determine if oil >10% (average) or >15% in any single year (oil-fired EGU threshold).

Calculate the capacity factor for oil = (total annual heat input from oil) / (maximum hourly heat input regardless of fuel × 8,760) for each year and for the required 24-month contiguous averaging block, and determine whether the oil capacity factor averaged over that 24-month period is < 8%.
Determine whether the unit has the capability (permit and on-site fuel handling) to combust coal or other fossil fuels (to evaluate 'fossil fuel-fired' capability in definitions).

Determine the proportion of fuel that is natural gas (annual heat input basis) to check whether the unit may instead meet the natural gas-fired EGU or the 85% natural gas criterion referenced by subpart DDDDD.
Verify the applicable compliance date and the 24-month averaging start point (see § 63.9984) for computing the limited-use 24-month block.

Confirm whether the unit has been permanently converted (permit or physical limitation) to natural gas or biomass after its compliance date (possible basis for being no longer subject to subpart UUUUU per § 63.9983(n)).
Check whether the unit is an IGCC or burns solid oil-derived fuel (these are separately categorized in § 63.9990 and § 63.10042).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key reasons from the EPA notes are captured: the answer includes the oil-fired EGU determination (oil as primary fuel per 40 CFR 63.10042/63.9990 thresholds) and the limited-use liquid oil-fired subcategory criterion (the <8% oil capacity-factor over the specified 24-month block), so the EPA's stated basis is reflected in the criteria."}

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Coating Manufacturing Operations

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous coating manufacturing operations that are located at or are part of a major source, manufacture coatings, process, use, or produce HAP, and are not part of an affected source under another subpart, then the operations are subject to this subpart.

If a material is produced by a process where a formulation component is synthesized by chemical reaction or separation activity and then transferred to another vessel where it is formulated and the synthesized or separated component is not stored prior to formulation, then that material is not considered a 'coating' for purposes of this subpart.

If the operation is one of the listed exceptions (research and development facilities; affiliated operations located at affected sources under specified subparts; ancillary equipment not directly involved in manufacturing; QA/QC labs; or modifying a purchased coating in preparation for application at the purchasing facility), then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to that operation.

If you use control devices or closed-vent systems to meet emission limits specified in this subpart, then you must comply with the subpart's monitoring, compliance, and closed-vent/control-device requirements.

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing Process Units (MCPU)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process unit (MCPU) that is located at or is part of a major source, the MCPU produces materials described by the listed SIC/NAICS codes or specified product types, the MCPU processes, uses, or generates organic HAP or hydrogen halide and halogen HAP, and the MCPU is not an affected source or part of an affected source under another subpart, then the subpart applies.

If the operation is an affiliated operation located at an affected source under the listed subparts (e.g., mixing or dissolving of coating ingredients; coating mixing for viscosity adjustment; cleaning of coating lines; handling and storage of coatings and solvent; conveyance and treatment of wastewater), then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to those affiliated operations.

If filtration is performed as a unit operation (filtration equipment is a listed unit operation) or as a separation, purification, or other processing step that is part of producing a product or isolated intermediate, then that filtration is a process step to be considered in determining whether the activity is part of an MCPU.

checklist: Is the facility a major source of HAP (per CAA section 112(a))?
Does the operation manufacture a 'coating' as defined in 40 CFR 63.8105 (i.e., a material intended to be applied to a substrate and produced by blending/mixing/diluting/formulating)?

Does the process 'synthesize' or 'separate' a formulation component (including by filtration) that is then transferred to another vessel and formulated into the final material, and is that synthesized/separated component stored prior to formulation or not?
Is the final filtration step a unit operation that separates/purifies a component (e.g., filtrate vs. solids) rather than merely removing lumps/gels as a final quality-control pass?
Are HAP present in feedstocks, intermediates, or products (identify which HAP and approximate concentrations and mass flowrates)?

Is the activity classified under the SIC/NAICS codes listed for coatings (e.g., NAICS 325510, 325520, 325910) or under the organic chemical manufacturing codes referenced in subpart FFFF (e.g., NAICS 325 series)?

Are the process vessels, tanks, filters, or storage tanks assigned to an existing affected source under another Part 63 subpart (i.e., are they 'affiliated operations' of another regulated affected source)?
Are routine cleaning operations part of the batch operations (would they be considered part of the process) or are they purely ancillary/closed-system equipment?
Are storage tanks, transfer racks, or loading arms predominantly used for coating operations or for an MCPU (determine predominant use per the applicable assignment procedures)?

What are the capacities of vessels/filters (e.g., are process vessels ≥250 gal) and do they meet definitions that would categorize them as process vessels or storage tanks under the coating subpart or MCPU subpart?

Are emissions from the filtration step or associated vents likely to contain organic HAP at levels that would constitute process vents, wastewater, or otherwise subject equipment under either subpart?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The answer includes the 63.8105 separation-activity criterion and an explicit checklist question about whether final filtration is a separation vs. a QC pass (capturing EPA’s finding that final filtering is not a ‘separation activity’), it lists HHHHH applicability when HAP-containing materials/solvents are used, and it cites the FFFF provisions/exclusions for affiliated/coating operations (63.2435 citations). Thus the key reasons in the EPA notes are represented."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Petroleum Refineries

criteria.criterion: If a combustion device lacks an enclosed combustion chamber and uses an uncontrolled volume of ambient air to burn gases, then it is a flare for purposes of this subpart.

If the truck-loading-rack vapors constitute a miscellaneous process vent that meets the Group 1 thresholds (organic HAP ≥ 20 ppmv and TOC emissions ≥ 33 kg/day for existing sources or ≥ 6.8 kg/day for new sources at the outlet of the final recovery device), then the vent is a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent and must be controlled by either a flare meeting § 63.670 or an alternate control achieving 98% reduction or 20 ppmv.

If the control device is an enclosed combustion device (for example an incinerator, boiler, or process heater with an enclosed combustion chamber), then that device is not a flare and the monitoring requirements in § 63.644 for enclosed devices (e.g., temperature monitoring for incinerators or boilers/process heaters) apply instead of the flare-specific requirements in § 63.670.

If the owner/operator elects to reduce emissions from a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent using a flare, then the flare must meet the requirements of § 63.670 (including pilot-flame, visible-emissions, tip-velocity/NHV limits, and associated monitoring) and associated CPMS requirements in § 63.671.

If the vent stream is routed to the refinery fuel gas system (i.e., not open to the atmosphere), then that stream is excluded from the definition of miscellaneous process vent under this subpart (but any flares receiving gas from the fuel gas system must comply with § 63.670 on and after January 30, 2019).

checklist: Determine whether the vapor combustor has an enclosed combustion chamber (physical drawings/specifications of the unit; photos of tip/stack and combustion chamber).
Determine whether the unit relies on uncontrolled ambient air at an open tip to support combustion (presence of open flare tip, lack of enclosed firebox/stack dampers or controlled combustion air).

Identify whether the loading-rack vapor stream is a miscellaneous process vent and whether it meets Group 1 criteria: measure organic HAP concentration (ppmv) and calculate TOC or organic HAP mass flow (kg/day) at the outlet of any recovery device.

Verify whether the loading-rack vapors are routed to a closed vent/fuel gas system or directly to the combustor (piping diagrams, process flow diagrams, valves showing closed-vent routing versus direct discharge).

Confirm the design and intended function of the combustor (manufacturer data/spec sheet): is it labeled/designed as a flare, thermal oxidizer/incinerator, boiler or process heater, or other enclosed device? Show whether primary function is energy recovery (boiler/heater) or open disposal (flare).

If the device appears to be a flare, verify presence and design of typical flare features: flare tip geometry, assist steam/air capability, pilot flame system, and whether the unit lacks an enclosed firebox.

If considering the device as a boiler/process heater, confirm whether vent streams are introduced into the flame zone (and the unit's design heat input capacity) per § 63.644 to determine applicable monitoring.
Establish whether regulated material is or will be routed to the device on/after January 30, 2019 (affects whether § 63.670 applies to flares receiving fuel-gas-system gas).

Collect piping diagrams showing boundaries of flare/gas streams and any crossovers, to support any eligibility for fixed-net-heating-value monitoring exemptions or to identify monitoring locations per § 63.670(j).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key EPA reasons are present: the answer cites the §63.641 flare definition (distinguishing flares from enclosed combustion devices), states enclosed combustors are not flares and are subject to §63.644 monitoring (not §63.670/63.671), and the checklist includes verifying enclosed design and applicable testing/monitoring to demonstrate compliance with subpart CC."}

candidates.title: Paper and Other Web Coating Operations

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a major source of HAP and operates web coating lines, then the provisions of this subpart apply to the facility.

If a coating operation is a web coating line, defined as one or more work stations that apply a continuous layer of liquid or semi-liquid coating material across the entire width or any portion of the width of a web substrate with associated curing/drying equipment between an unwind or feed station and a rewind or cutting station, then that operation meets the subpart's definition of a web coating line.
If the substrate is not a web (i.e., not a continuous substrate flexible enough to be wound or unwound as rolls), then that operation is not a web coating line under this subpart.

If a web coating line falls into any of the exclusions listed in paragraphs (a) through (g) (for example, stand-alone equipment under subpart KK, product and packaging rotogravure or wide-web flexographic presses under subpart KK, certain printing processes, lines subject to subparts EE, SSSS, or OOOO, or research or laboratory equipment), then that line is not part of the affected source under this subpart.

If a web coating line coats both paper (or a web) and another substrate, then the subpart that applies is determined by the predominant activity (90 percent or more of the mass of substrate coated during the compliance period), with the predominant-activity subpart governing applicability.

If a web coating line subject to this subpart is modified to include printing activities, then the owner/operator may elect to continue demonstrating compliance with this subpart instead of subpart KK if the mass applied at the line's print station(s) in a month ever exceeds 5 percent of the total mass applied to the line during the same period.

If all of the subject web coating lines at the facility utilize only non-HAP coatings and a one-time report as required in §63.3370(s) documenting use of only non-HAP coatings is submitted to the permitting authority, then the facility can be exempt from the reporting requirements of this subpart.

If an affected source is subject to this subpart, then it must meet the organic HAP emission limits and related compliance requirements specified in §63.3320 on and after the applicable compliance dates.

If the source is an existing versus new affected source (construction or reconstruction commenced on or before September 13, 2000 or after), then different numeric monthly limits and percent-reduction targets in §63.3320(b) apply.

checklist: Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAP as defined in 40 CFR 63.2.
For each mica line, verify whether the substrate is a web (continuous, flexible, windable) or individual sheets (not a web).

For each mica line, verify whether the operation includes an unwind/feed station and a rewind/cutting station and whether coatings are applied as a continuous liquid or semi-liquid layer across any portion of the web width.
Determine whether any line meets any exclusion in 40 CFR 63.3300(a)–(g) (e.g., is covered by subpart KK, EE, SSSS, OOOO, is research/lab equipment, or is a printing process listed there).

If a line coats mixed substrates (paper/web plus other substrates), calculate the mass of substrate coated by type over a representative period (at least one year or an alternative reasonable period) to determine whether paper/web constitutes ≥90 percent of the mass (predominant activity) per 40 CFR 63.3300(h).
If printing was added, calculate monthly mass applied at the line's print station(s) as a percent of the total mass applied to the line to evaluate the 5% condition in 40 CFR 63.3300(i).
Check whether all coatings used on the subject web coating lines are non-HAP and, if so, prepare the one-time report required by §63.3370(s) to claim the reporting exemption under 40 CFR 63.3300(j).
Determine whether each affected source is 'existing' or 'new' (construction/reconstruction commenced on or before September 13, 2000 or after) to know which numeric limits in 40 CFR 63.3320(b) apply.

If subject to the subpart, assemble records and procedures to demonstrate compliance with the monthly organic HAP limits and the compliance procedures referenced in §63.3370 as required by 40 CFR 63.3320.

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"The answer includes the web-coating criteria (definition of a web, unwind/feed and rewind/cutting, and checklist to verify roll-fed vs sheets) that capture EPA’s reason for JJJJ applying to the roll-fed line and not the sheet line, but it omits any criteria or citation regarding the refractory-product definition (40 CFR 63.9824) and the basis for concluding the mica insulation is not a refractory product (SSSSS), so that key reason is missing."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Glycol Dehydration Units (Natural Gas Transmission and Storage)

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a natural gas transmission and storage facility that is a major source and contains a glycol dehydration unit, then subpart HHH applies to that glycol dehydration unit (affected source).

If you intend to use a boiler or process heater as the control device for a glycol dehydration unit process vent, then the process vent must be connected to that boiler or process heater through a closed‑vent system and the vent stream shall be introduced into the flame zone of the boiler or process heater.

If the closed‑vent system routes gases, vapors, and fumes from the emissions unit to the control device it must be designed and operated with no detectable emissions; conversely, if the glycol vent gas is routed to a process or reused (for example injected into the flame zone or sent to a fuel gas system), then the conveyance/recovery system is not considered a closed‑vent system or a control device for purposes of this subpart.

If an enclosed combustion device (including a boiler or process heater) is used as the control device it must achieve the subpart HHH performance requirements (e.g., 95% reduction or ≤20 ppmv TOC at 3% O2 or operate at ≥760°C where demonstrated) and must be operating whenever gases are vented through the closed‑vent system.

If the combustion unit’s primary purpose is to transfer heat to a process fluid (e.g., glycol) rather than to generate steam or hot water, then it meets the definition of a process heater; if its primary purpose is steam or hot water generation it meets the definition of a boiler.

candidates.title: General Provisions (as referenced by Subpart HHH)

criteria.criterion: If Table 2 of subpart HHH specifies particular subpart A (General Provisions) sections as applicable, then those specific subpart A provisions apply to owners/operators of affected sources as indicated in Table 2.

checklist: Is your facility a natural gas transmission and storage facility located within the site boundaries used for the major source determination? (see 40 CFR 63.1270(a))
Is the facility a major source of HAP (calculate PTE or actual emissions to determine major source status used by 40 CFR 63.1270)?
Does the facility have a glycol dehydration unit (per 40 CFR 63.1271 definition) and is it designated an affected source at this site?
Is the glycol dehydration unit a large or small unit (calculate actual annual average natural gas flowrate and benzene emissions per 40 CFR 63.1271 definitions)?
Where does the glycol dehydration unit reboiler vent (still vent) actually route (flare, closed‑vent to control device, fuel gas system, direct to atmosphere)?

If the still vent is routed to a combustion unit (your reboiler burner), is the vent stream physically introduced into the flame zone of that combustion unit, or is the combustion unit simply exhausting separately to atmosphere? (key for being a control device per 40 CFR 63.1281(d)(1)(i)(D) and 40 CFR 63.1275(b)(1)(i))

Is the conduit from the dehydration unit to the combustion device a closed‑vent system designed and operated with no detectable emissions (or is the stream routed to a process/fuel gas system such that it is not treated as a closed‑vent system per 40 CFR 63.1281(c)(2) and 63.1271)?

Is the vent gas being used/reused (e.g., sent to a fuel gas system or injected as fuel) rather than being routed to a control device for destruction? (if yes, note the conveyance may not be a control device/closed‑vent per 40 CFR 63.1271)
What is the primary purpose of the combustion unit (heat glycol/process fluid vs. steam/hot water generation) to classify it as a process heater or boiler per 40 CFR 63.1271 definitions?

Is the combustion device operated whenever the unit vents (i.e., continuously available to receive the vent) and can it meet the HHH performance requirements (95% reduction, ≤20 ppmv TOC at 3% O2, or ≥760°C where applicable) per 40 CFR 63.1281(d) and 63.1281(d)(4)(i)?
Are there bypasses, valves, or practices that would divert vent gas away from the combustion device (check for bypass devices and closed‑vent securement/alarms per 40 CFR 63.1281(c)(3))?
Check Table 2 in Subpart HHH to identify which subpart A general provisions apply at your site (40 CFR 63.1274(a)).

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"Some key points are captured (the checklist asks where the still vent actually routes and whether the vent is introduced into the flame zone, and the criteria include the process‑heater vs boiler classification), but the EPA’s core determination that HHH only covers the still vent/flash tank (not the reboiler exhaust) and that the reboiler, as an uncontrolled process heater whose fuel is not regulated by another subpart, is therefore subject to the Boiler/Process Heater MACT (DDDDD) are not explicitly included."}
