candidates.title: Surface Coating of Miscellaneous Metal Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a source that uses 946 liters (250 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain hazardous air pollutants (HAP) in the surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and products and the source is a major source (or is located at or part of a major source), then the source is subject to this subpart.

If the coating operation is the application of coatings to substrates (for example by spray guns or dip tanks) and is not limited to handheld non-refillable aerosol containers, touch-up markers, marking pens, or application of pre-coated paper or plastic film, then the activity qualifies as a surface coating operation under this subpart.

If the facility uses only coatings, thinners, additives, and cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP (as determined under § 63.3941(a)), then this subpart does not apply to the surface coating operations.

If individual coatings are used in volumes of less than 189 liters (50 gallons) per year and the total volume of coatings exempt under that provision does not exceed 946 liters (250 gallons) per year at the facility, then those coatings are exempt under this subpart.

If a coating meets the definition of rubber-to-metal coatings (i.e., contains heat-activated polymer systems in solvent or water that dry to a non-tacky surface and react chemically with rubber and metal during a vulcanization process), then that coating operation falls in the rubber-to-metal coatings subcategory.

If a coating does not meet the definitions of high performance coating, magnet wire coating, rubber-to-metal coating, or extreme performance fluoropolymer coating, then the coating operation is in the general use coating subcategory.

checklist: Is the part or product you coat a 'miscellaneous metal part or product' as described in 40 CFR 63.3881(a)?
Is the coating applied by surface coating methods (spray, dip, etc.) rather than by handheld non-refillable aerosol containers, touch-up markers, marking pens, or pre-coated film?
What is the annual volume (liters or gallons) of coatings that contain organic HAP used in the metal surface coating operations (total at the facility and by individual coating)?
Is the facility a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥10 tons/year of any single HAP or ≥25 tons/year of combined HAP), or is it located at or part of a major source?
Do the coatings, thinners, additives, or cleaning materials contain any organic HAP (verify manufacturer formulation data or testing per § 63.3941)?

For the coating in question, does the formulation contain a heat-activated polymer system and, when cured, does it dry to a non-tacky surface and react chemically with rubber and metal during a vulcanization process (i.e., does the bonding step involve vulcanization of rubber)?

If bonding occurs during heating but you do not use vulcanization of rubber, document whether the chemical reaction meets the rubber-to-metal definition (heat-activated polymer that reacts during a vulcanization process) or not.
Are any individual coatings used <189 liters (50 gallons)/year and does the total of such exempt coatings remain ≤946 liters (250 gallons)/year at the facility?
Do any coatings meet definitions for other subcategories (magnet wire, high performance, or extreme performance fluoropolymer) that would change subcategory assignment?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's sole key reason — the bonding is not performed during a vulcanization process, so it does not meet the rubber-to-metal coating definition — is explicitly captured by the provided criteria and checklist (notably the rubber-to-metal definition criterion and checklist items about whether bonding involves vulcanization)."}

candidates.title: Wool fiberglass manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If the product is bonded wool fiberglass with a loss on ignition of less than 8 percent and a density of less than 32 kilograms per cubic meter, then it meets this subpart's definition of "building insulation."
If the owner or operator's wool fiberglass manufacturing facility is a major source or is located at a facility that is a major source, then the requirements of this subpart apply to that facility.
If a rotary spin wool fiberglass manufacturing line produces a bonded wool fiberglass building insulation product, then the requirements of this subpart apply to that manufacturing line.
If a flame attenuation wool fiberglass manufacturing line produces a bonded product, then the requirements of this subpart apply to that manufacturing line.
If there is a glass-melting furnace at the wool fiberglass manufacturing facility, then the requirements of this subpart apply to each new and existing glass-melting furnace at the facility.

If you need to determine product loss on ignition or density for classification under this subpart, then you must use the test methods specified in this subpart (Appendix A for LOI and Appendix C for density) per §63.1385.

checklist: Is the product bonded wool fiberglass (i.e., glass fibers with a phenol-formaldehyde binder applied)?
Measure the product LOI using Appendix A to Subpart NNN and confirm whether LOI < 8%.
Measure the product density using Appendix C to Subpart NNN and confirm whether density < 32 kg/m^3 (2 lb/ft^3).
Which forming process is used for the product: rotary spin or flame attenuation?
If rotary spin, is the line specifically producing a bonded building insulation product?
If flame attenuation, is the product a bonded product produced on that line?
Does the facility (or the facility where the line is located) qualify as a major source under 40 CFR 63.2?
Are any lines operated primarily (>=75% of annual operating hours) as aerospace, HVAC, or OEM product lines (these categories have separate definitions in §63.1381)?
Is there a glass-melting furnace at the facility that is new or existing (subject to the subpart's requirements)?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's note hinges solely on the product meeting Subpart NNN's definition of 'building insulation.' OUR ANSWER explicitly includes that criterion (bonded wool fiberglass with LOI <8% and density <32 kg/m^3, citing 40 CFR 63.1381) and includes the required test methods and checklist steps to demonstrate that, so the key reason is captured."}

candidates.title: Polyether polyol manufacturing (Subpart PPP)

criteria.criterion: If the plant site is a major source and a process unit's primary product is a polyether polyol, then that process unit is a polyether polyol manufacturing process unit (PMPU) and, together with associated equipment, is an affected source subject to this subpart.

If a PMPU does not use or manufacture any organic HAP during the production of one or more products, then that PMPU is not subject to the provisions of this subpart except that the owner/operator must retain documentation supporting that determination and demonstrate it when requested, and the PMPU is not required to comply with Subpart A for that PMPU.

If a PMPU uses tetrahydrofuran (THF) to produce one or more polyether polyol products at an affected source, then each process vent at that PMPU must comply with the HON process vent requirements in §§ 63.113 through 63.118 as tailored by paragraph (f) of this section.

If epoxides are used in the production of polyether polyols at an affected source, then the owner/operator must follow the epoxide-specific process vent control requirements in § 63.1425(b) (including the options and control levels for new and existing affected sources).

If emissions from process vents, storage vessels, wastewater, or equipment leaks are combined and at least one of the included streams would require control absent the combination, then the owner/operator must either comply with the applicable requirements for each kind of emission or comply with the single most stringent set of requirements that applies to any individual stream in the combined flow.

If a process vent uses a combustion, recovery, or recapture device to meet the process vent control requirements, then the owner/operator must install, calibrate, maintain, and operate the monitoring equipment specified for that device in § 63.1429(a) (or approved alternative parameters), and operate it according to manufacturers' specifications or other adequate written procedures.

If a batch unit process vent has organic HAP emissions greater than 225 kg/yr (or, for continuous unit operations, the vent stream contains more than 0.005 weight-percent total organic HAP, or meets ethylene oxide criteria), then that vent meets the subpart's definition of a process vent and must be evaluated under the process vent provisions unless an exclusion applies.

If a process vent is used only as a result of start-up, shutdown, maintenance, or inspection and meets the maintenance vent criteria, then the owner/operator may designate it as a maintenance vent and it will be subject only to the maintenance vent provisions in § 63.1425(h) and the referenced recordkeeping and reporting requirements.

If a closed vent system or control device has bypass lines that could divert emissions to the atmosphere, then the owner/operator must either install and operate a flow indicator at the bypass or secure the bypass valve with a car-seal/lock-and-key and perform the required inspections, and after the specified compliance dates bypassing to atmosphere or to non‑conforming devices is an emissions standards violation.

checklist: Determine whether the plant site qualifies as a major source under the Major Source definition (Subpart A) for HAP.
Determine the primary product of the specific process unit (use the mass-based design capacity and flexible-unit rules in 40 CFR 63.1420(e)).
Confirm whether the process unit is therefore a PMPU (primary product = polyether polyol) per 40 CFR 63.1420(e).
Verify whether tetrahydrofuran (THF) is used as a raw material in the PMPU for making polyether polyols for any operating campaigns.
Verify whether THF (or any other chemicals used or produced in the process) is listed as an organic HAP in table 4 of Subpart PPP or otherwise qualifies as an organic HAP under the subpart.
Determine whether any organic HAPs are used or knowingly produced (other than as impurities) in the PMPU, including during any catalyst extraction or other steps.
If the unit uses epoxides, document which epoxides and whether process vents would be subject to § 63.1425(b) control options.
Establish whether the polymerization reactor and associated vents are operated as batch or continuous unit operations.

For each vent, calculate annual organic HAP emissions, vent flow rates, and organic HAP concentrations to determine whether vents meet the process vent thresholds (batch: >225 kg/yr; continuous: >0.005 wt-% TOC or EO criteria) per 40 CFR 63.1423.
Identify whether any emissions streams (process vents, storage vessels, wastewater, equipment leaks) are combined and, if so, determine which stream(s) would require control absent the combination.
List all process vents and note whether they route to combustion, recovery, or recapture devices (type of device for each vent).

If controls are present or planned, identify the specific control device types (flare, incinerator/catalytic incinerator, boiler/process heater, absorber, condenser, carbon adsorber, recovery system) to determine required monitoring parameters under § 63.1429(a).

Check whether any catalyst is used or catalyst extraction occurs in the process (user stated no catalyst; verify), since catalyst extraction with nonepoxide organic HAPs triggers § 63.1425(d) requirements.

Document and retain the information/records and analyses that demonstrate that the PMPU does not use or manufacture organic HAP (if claiming exemption under § 63.1420(b)(1)), and be prepared to demonstrate this to the Administrator on request.

If planning to designate any vent as a maintenance vent, confirm the start-up/shutdown/maintenance-only nature and verify compliance with the specific pre‑venting purging, pressure, mass, and measurement requirements in § 63.1425(h).

candidates.title: Paper and Other Web Coating

criteria.criterion: if your facility is a major source of HAP and web coating lines are operated at the facility then this subpart applies (subject).

if the operation between an unwind/feed station and a rewind/cutting station includes one or more work stations that apply a continuous layer of liquid or semi-liquid material across the width (and any associated curing/drying equipment) then that operation meets the definition of a web coating line and is part of the affected source of this subpart (subject when the facility is a major source of HAP).

if a web coating line is stand-alone equipment that is included in the affected source under subpart KK by the owner/operator then that line is not part of the affected source of this subpart (not subject).

if a web coating line is a product and packaging rotogravure or wide-web flexographic press that is included in the affected source under subpart KK then that line is not part of the affected source of this subpart (not subject).
if the coating activity is lithography, screenprinting, letterpress, or narrow-web flexographic printing then that web coating is not part of the affected source of this subpart (not subject).
if a web coating line is already subject to subpart EE then it is not part of the affected source of this subpart (not subject).
if a web coating line is already subject to subpart SSSS then it is not part of the affected source of this subpart (not subject).
if a web coating line is already subject to subpart OOOO then it is not part of the affected source of this subpart (not subject).
if the equipment is research or laboratory equipment as defined in §63.3310 then the web coating line is not part of the affected source of this subpart (not subject).

if a web coating line coats both paper (or another web) and another substrate then the applicable subpart is determined by the predominant activity: if 90 percent or more of the mass of substrate coated during the compliance period is paper then this subpart applies, otherwise this subpart does not apply to that line (subject/not subject determined by 90% mass rule; predominant activity must be demonstrated annually).

if a web coating line with product and packaging rotogravure or wide-web flexographic print station(s) has the mass of materials applied to its print station(s) in a month ever exceed 5 percent of the total mass applied to the line in that month then the owner/operator may elect to continue demonstrating compliance with this subpart instead of subpart KK (subjectness may be elected).

if all of the subject web coating lines at the facility utilize only non-HAP coatings and you submit the one-time report required in §63.3370(s) then you can be exempt from the reporting requirements of this subpart (not subject to reporting).

if the materials applied are adhesives (including hot melt adhesives) or other liquid or semi-liquid materials then those materials are 'coating materials' for this subpart and count toward making an operation a web coating line (relevant to subjectness).

if the materials applied are only applied via vapor deposition or are dry abrasive materials (or are materials used solely to form a substrate) then they are not 'coating materials' for this subpart and the operation is not a web coating line for purposes of this subpart (not subject).

checklist: Is the facility a major source of HAP (check facility-wide PTE and actual emissions relative to major source thresholds)?

Does the operation include an unwind/feed station, continuous application of a liquid or semi-liquid material (e.g., glue/adhesive) at one or more work stations, any curing/drying equipment, and a rewind or cutting station (i.e., does it meet the 'web coating line' definition)?
Are the materials you apply (adhesives/glue) considered coating materials or are they applied by vapor deposition or as dry abrasives (which are excluded)?

Do any web coating lines at the facility fall under the listed exclusions: stand-alone equipment included under subpart KK, product/packaging rotogravure or wide-web flexographic presses included under subpart KK, lithography/screenprinting/letterpress/narrow-web flexographic printing, subpart EE, subpart SSSS, or subpart OOOO?

If a line coats multiple substrate types, what is the mass fraction (over a representative compliance period of at least one year or another reasonable period) of paper/web substrate vs. other substrates (is paper ≥90% by mass)?

Do any lines have product and packaging rotogravure or wide-web flexographic print stations and, if so, does the monthly mass applied to print stations ever exceed 5% of the total mass applied to the line (to evaluate the §63.3300(i) election)?
Are any lines operated as research or laboratory equipment under the definition in §63.3310?
Do all subject web coating lines use only non-HAP coatings (and if so, can you prepare and submit the one-time report required by §63.3370(s))?

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Wood Furniture Manufacturing Operations

criteria.criterion: if the facility is engaged, either in part or in whole, in the manufacture of wood furniture or wood furniture components and is located at a plant site that is a major source, then the source is an affected source under this subpart

if the owner or operator of the source uses no more than 250 gallons per month (for every month) of coating, gluing, cleaning, and washoff materials at the source (including materials used for source categories other than wood furniture), then the source is an area source for purposes of this subpart and is not subject to any other provision of this subpart

if the owner or operator of the source uses no more than 3,000 gallons per rolling 12-month period of coating, gluing, cleaning, and washoff materials at the source (including materials used for source categories other than wood furniture), then the source is an area source for purposes of this subpart and is not subject to any other provision of this subpart

if the source emits no more than 4.5 Mg (5 tons) of any one HAP per rolling 12-month period and no more than 11.4 Mg (12.5 tons) of any combination of HAP per rolling 12-month period, and at least 90 percent of plantwide emissions per rolling 12-month period are associated with manufacture of wood furniture or components, then the source is an area source for purposes of this subpart and is not subject to any other provision of this subpart

if the surface coating operation is surface coating of metal components of wood furniture performed at a wood furniture or wood furniture component manufacturing facility, then those metal-component coating operations are subject to subpart JJ (not excluded)

if the surface coating operation is surface coating of metal furniture that meets the applicability criteria for subpart RRRR (metal furniture surface coating), then that surface coating operation is excluded from subpart JJ

if the surface coating of metal parts and products is of items other than metal components of wood furniture and meets the applicability criteria for miscellaneous metal parts and products surface coating (subpart MMMM), then that surface coating operation is excluded from subpart JJ

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Surface Coating of Metal Furniture

criteria.criterion: if the operation is surface coating of metal furniture (coating applied to metal furniture or components as defined), then the operation falls within the source category to which this subpart applies

if you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source as defined in §63.4882 in the metal furniture surface coating source category and that affected source is a major source, is located at a major source, or is part of a major source of HAP, then you are subject to this subpart
if the surface coating uses only coatings, thinners, and cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP, then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart

if the surface coating of metal components of wood furniture is conducted in an operation that is subject to the wood furniture manufacturing NESHAP (subpart JJ), then subpart RRRR does not apply to those coatings

if the surface coating is conducted for the purpose of repairing or maintaining metal furniture used by a major source and not for commerce, then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart unless organic HAP emissions from the coating are high enough to meet the major-source thresholds in paragraph (b)

if the collection of all coating operations, storage containers, mixing vessels, conveying equipment, pumps, piping, and waste material handling used for surface coating of metal furniture at the plant meet the definition of an affected source in §63.4882, then those items are within the regulated affected source under this subpart

checklist: Confirm whether the plant site is a major source of HAP (emit or potential to emit ≥ 10 tons/year of a single HAP or ≥ 25 tons/year combined HAP).
Confirm that the facility is engaged in manufacture of wood furniture or wood furniture components (i.e., wood furniture manufacturing operations are present).

Determine whether the metal items you coat are metal components of wood furniture (parts intended for use in the wood furniture you manufacture) or are separate metal equipment/parts not used as furniture components.
For the metal coating activities, confirm whether the coated items meet the definition of "metal furniture" or "metal furniture components" used in Subpart RRRR/63.4881.

Calculate and document total gallons of coatings, thinners, cleaning, gluing, and washoff materials used at the entire plant by month (include materials used for non-wood-furniture categories), to compare to the 250 gallons-per-month threshold in 63.800(b)(1).

Calculate and document total gallons of coatings, thinners, cleaning, gluing, and washoff materials used at the entire plant on a rolling 12-month basis to compare to the 3,000 gallons-per-rolling-12-month threshold in 63.800(b)(2).
Calculate plantwide HAP emissions on a rolling 12-month basis (tons or Mg) for each individual HAP and for combined HAP to compare to 4.5 Mg (5 t) and 11.4 Mg (12.5 t) thresholds in 63.800(b)(3).

Determine what fraction (percent) of plantwide HAP emissions are associated with wood furniture finishing materials, adhesives, cleaning, and washoff operations to evaluate the 90% criterion in 63.800(b).
Verify whether the metal-coating materials used contain any organic HAP (if they contain no organic HAP, Subpart RRRR may not apply per 63.4881(c)(1)).
Confirm whether the metal coating work is performed as facility maintenance/repair not for commerce (and quantify emissions) to evaluate the §63.4881(c)(5) maintenance exclusion.
Confirm whether metal-component coating activities are performed at the wood furniture manufacturing facility (if so, Subpart JJ may cover them per 63.800(d)(4) and 63.4881(c)(2)).
Verify recordkeeping: maintain monthly usage records and, if relying on area-source volume limits, retain these records for at least five years as required by 63.800(b)(1) and (b)(2).
Clarify units and time basis (user-reported "just under 250 gallons per year" must be compared to the 250 gallons per month threshold in 63.800(b)(1)).
Identify whether any control systems are used to limit emissions and whether the plant desires/needs to consider the affirmative defense provisions in 63.800(j) (if relevant).

The checklist also requires determining whether coated items are furniture components, so the exclusion rationale is captured."}

candidates.title: Printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, and finishing of fabric and other textiles

criteria.criterion: If you perform printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, or finishing of fabric or other textiles at your facility and you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source that is a major source, is located at a major source, or is part of a major source, then you are subject to this subpart.
If your facility does not perform any printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, or finishing operations on fabric or other textiles as defined in this subpart, then you are not subject to this subpart.

If your coating, printing, slashing, dyeing, or finishing operations use only regulated materials that contain no organic HAP (per the 'No organic HAP' definition), then those operations are not subject to this subpart.
If the operations are research or laboratory operations or are part of janitorial, building, and facility maintenance operations, then those operations are not subject to this subpart.
If the operations are used by the facility and not for commerce (unless organic HAP emissions from those operations reach major source levels), then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If web coating or printing operations are conducted at ambient temperatures and do not involve drying or curing equipment such as ovens, tenter frames, steam cans, or dryers, then those web coating or printing operations are not subject to this subpart.
If the operations are performed on-site at installations owned or operated by the Armed Forces of the United States, then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If the activities at issue do not meet the affected source definitions for the web coating and printing, slashing, or dyeing and finishing subcategories (i.e., do not include the equipment, containers, or regulated materials listed for an affected source), then they are not part of an affected source covered by this subpart.

If the materials and processes you use do not meet the definitions of coating, printing, dyeing, finishing, or slashing in § 63.4371 (for example, the applied material is not a semi-liquid that dries to form a continuous solid film for coatings, or printing/dyeing as defined is not occurring), then those activities are not subject to this subpart.

checklist: Confirm whether the shoelace tipping operation is characterized as printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, or finishing per the definitions in 40 CFR 63.4371 (does the applied material form a continuous solid film; is color/pattern applied; is fiber chemically finished; etc.).
Determine whether the substrate (shoelaces/thread) qualifies as 'fabric' or 'textile' under the definitions in 40 CFR 63.4371.

Determine whether the operation is performed on a web (continuous textile substrate) or on discrete items (e.g., individual shoelace tips), and whether it is part of a web coating/printing line as described in §63.4282.

Identify all materials used in the tipping operation (including the methanol solution and any additives) and obtain manufacturer's formulation data to determine whether they are regulated materials (coating, printing, thinning, cleaning, slashing, dyeing, or finishing materials).
Calculate the organic HAP content (mass fraction) of each regulated material used to determine if they meet the 'No organic HAP' thresholds in the subpart definitions.
Confirm whether any drying or curing equipment (ovens, dryers, tenter frames, steam cans, or similar) is used during or after the tipping process.
Determine whether the operation is research/laboratory, janitorial/maintenance, or a non-commercial activity (and whether emissions would nonetheless meet major source levels).

Determine whether the affected source (as defined in §63.4282) at your facility is a major source of HAPs, or is located at or part of a major source (verify facility-wide HAP emissions against the major source thresholds per 40 CFR part 63/§63.2).
Verify whether the operation is performed at an Armed Forces installation (exemption in §63.4281(c)(5)).
If your facility also coats or prints other substrates, determine the predominant activity by mass of substrate coated (90% rule) to see which subpart applies (see §63.4281(e)).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Halogenated Solvent Cleaning

criteria.criterion: If a device uses any of the listed halogenated HAP solvents (methylene chloride, perchloroethylene, trichloroethylene, 1,1,1-trichloroethane, carbon tetrachloride, or chloroform) in a total concentration greater than 5 percent by weight as a cleaning or drying agent, then subject to Subpart T.
If a device uses halogenated HAP solvent liquid or vapor to remove soils (i.e., meets the definition of a solvent cleaning machine), then it is a solvent cleaning machine for purposes of Subpart T.
If the cleaning machine is an immersion batch cold cleaning machine (parts immersed in liquid solvent during cleaning), then the batch cold cleaning machine standards in §63.462 apply.

If the cleaning machine is a batch vapor or an in-line cleaning machine, then the design, operational and control requirements in §63.463 apply unless the owner/operator elects to comply with the alternative standards in §63.464.

If the cleaning machine has a solvent/air interface, then the alternative standards in §63.464(a)(1) (emission limits per unit solvent/air interface area in table 5 and associated logging/monitoring) apply if the owner/operator elects to use §63.464.

If the cleaning machine is a batch vapor cleaning machine and does not have a solvent/air interface, then the alternative standards in §63.464(a)(2) apply (log of solvent additions/deletions and emissions limits determined by table 6 or equation 1 based on cleaning capacity).

If the cleaning machine is a continuous web or remote-reservoir continuous web cleaning machine, then the specific continuous-web requirements and allowed control combinations in §63.463(g) and (h) apply (including options for freeboard refrigeration, superheated vapor/part technology, carbon adsorbers, or demonstrating ≥70% overall control).

checklist: List all solvents used in the machine and confirm % by weight of listed halogenated HAPs to determine whether concentration > 5% (per 40 CFR 63.460(a)).
Determine whether the machine is a solvent cleaning machine under the definition (uses halogenated solvent liquid or vapor to remove soils) (40 CFR 63.461).
Classify the machine type: batch cold (immersion), batch vapor, in-line (including remote reservoir or continuous web), or continuous web (40 CFR 63.461; 63.462; 63.463).

Confirm whether parts are immersed in liquid solvent during cleaning (immersion) or whether cleaning uses vapor, or both (to distinguish cold vs vapor and immersion vs non-immersion) (40 CFR 63.461; 63.462).

Verify presence or absence of a solvent/air interface (for vapor machines the midline of primary condenser; for cold machines the liquid surface) and, if absent, measure the cleaning capacity (chamber volume) (40 CFR 63.461; 63.464(a)(2)).
Measure the solvent/air interface area (or cleaning capacity) to determine which emission limits or tables apply (table 5 uses area; table 6/equation 1 use cleaning capacity) (40 CFR 63.464; 63.461).
Determine whether the machine is new or existing (construction/reconstruction date relative to November 29, 1993) for applicability of certain compliance dates and provisions (40 CFR 63.460(c),(d)).

Identify installed controls and features (covers, freeboard ratio and freeboard height, freeboard refrigeration device / primary condenser, automated parts handling speed, lip exhaust, carbon adsorber, superheated vapor or part technology) to evaluate which §63.463 control options are feasible (40 CFR 63.463(a),(d),(e),(g)).

If electing the §63.464 alternative: be prepared to maintain logs of solvent additions/deletions and calculate/monthly demonstrate 3-month rolling average emissions per §63.464 and §63.465 (40 CFR 63.464(a),(b)).
Determine whether the facility is an area source or major source (may affect certain requirements and permit obligations referenced in §63.460(h) and (i)).

Our answer includes the controlling definition and thresholds (use of listed halogenated HAPs >5% and the solvent-cleaning-machine definition at 40 CFR 63.460/63.461) that capture that key reason."}

candidates.title: Printing, Coating, Slashing, Dyeing, and Finishing of Fabric and Other Textiles

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source that performs printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, or finishing of fabric and other textiles and the affected source is a major source of HAP, then the source is subject to this subpart.

If the coating, printing, slashing, dyeing, or finishing operations use only regulated materials that contain no organic HAP (per the "no organic HAP" definition), then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If the operation is a dyeing or finishing affected source (i.e., the regulated materials are dyeing and finishing materials for the affected source), then any solvent that is part of the dyeing/finishing material as applied must be counted toward the mass fraction of organic HAP of that dyeing/finishing material and the mass fraction of organic HAP (including added solvent) must be less than or equal to the applicable emission limit in Table 1 to use the compliant material option.

If you add an organic solvent to a coating or printing material after receipt (a "thinning material"), then for web coating/printing affected sources the compliant material option requires that the thinning material contain no organic HAP.

If a web coating line coats both fabric/textiles and another substrate, then the predominant activity (90 percent by mass of substrate during the compliance period) determines which subpart applies and may make the line subject to a different subpart instead of this subpart.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Paper and Other Web Coating (Subpart JJJJ)

criteria.criterion: If a web coating operation is part of the affected source of subpart JJJJ (paper and other web coating), then that web coating operation is not part of Subpart OOOO.

candidates.title: NESHAP for Tire Manufacturing (Subpart XXXX)

criteria.criterion: If a web coating operation is part of the affected source of subpart XXXX (tire manufacturing/tire cord), then that web coating operation is not part of Subpart OOOO.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for the Printing and Publishing Industry (Subpart KK)

criteria.criterion: If a web coating line coats or prints fabric or other textiles for use in flexible packaging and is included in an affected source under subpart KK, then that web coating line is not part of Subpart OOOO.

checklist: Determine whether the operation is a web dyeing or finishing operation as defined in 40 CFR 63.4371 and whether the affected source elements listed in 40 CFR 63.4282(d)(1)-(5) exist at the plant.
Confirm whether the affected source is a major source of HAP (per 40 CFR 63.2) or is located at/part of a major source (40 CFR 63.4281(b)).
Verify whether the regulated materials used are "no organic HAP" by the definition in 40 CFR 63.4371 (check supplier formulation data or test results).

Determine whether the solvent is added to the finishing material before application (part of the material as-applied) or is added after receipt as a thinning material to a coating/printing material (see 40 CFR 63.4371 definitions).

If the solvent is part of the finishing material as-applied, calculate the mass fraction of organic HAP for the finishing material including the solvent (using supplier formulation data or test methods per 40 CFR 63.4321(e)) and compare to the applicable emission limit in Table 1 (40 CFR 63.4321(c)).

If relying on supplier/manufacturer formulation data for organic HAP content, retain the data and note that supplier data is acceptable per 40 CFR 63.4321(e)(1)(iv); if tests conflict, test results prevail per 40 CFR 63.4321(e).

If the solvent is a thinning material added after receipt to a coating/printing material, verify whether you plan to use the compliant material option and, if so, confirm that the thinning material contains no organic HAP (40 CFR 63.4321(a)).

Check whether the web coating line also coats other substrates (paper, tire cord, flexible packaging) and if so determine predominant activity (90% mass rule) to decide if subparts JJJJ, XXXX, or KK instead apply (40 CFR 63.4281(e) and 63.4281(d)(1)-(4)).

Confirm whether any exclusions apply (research/lab operations, facility-internal non-commerce use, ambient-temperature web coating without drying/curing equipment, Armed Forces installations) per 40 CFR 63.4281(c)(2)-(5).

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Wood Building Products

criteria.criterion: If you apply coatings (including adhesives) in finishing or laminating to products that contain more than 50 percent by weight wood or wood fiber (excluding glass) and that are used in the construction of residential, commercial, or institutional buildings (for example doors, windows, millwork, moulding, or trim), then your operations are within the source category to which this subpart applies.
citations: 40 CFR 63.4781 (definition of Coating; definition of Adhesive)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an affected source that uses 4,170 liters (1,100 gallons) per year or more of coatings in the wood building products source category and the source or facility is a major source (or located at or part of a major source of HAP), then the source is subject to this subpart.

If your surface coating activities meet any of the exclusion criteria in paragraphs (c)(1) through (c)(5) (e.g., coatings that are part of plywood/composite wood manufacturing covered by subpart DDDD, wood furniture manufacturing covered by subpart JJ, prefabricated/mobile home manufacture, noncommercial/hobby/research coating, or wood treatment by retort), then those coating operations are not subject to this subpart.

If you have an affected source as defined in §63.4682—that is, the collection of all coating operations and associated storage, mixing, conveyance, and waste-handling equipment used for surface coating of wood building products—then those items are the parts of your plant covered by this subpart.

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Miscellaneous Metal Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you perform surface coating (including associated surface preparation, cleaning, mixing, and storage) on miscellaneous metal parts or products (including metal components of products such as extruded aluminum structural components), then your operations fall within the source category covered by this subpart.

If you own or operate an affected source that uses 946 liters (250 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain HAP in the surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and the source or facility is a major source (or located at or part of a major source of HAP), then the source is subject to this subpart.

If the coatings you apply meet the definition of high performance architectural coating (e.g., coatings applied to architectural subsections required to meet AAMA 605.2-2000), then the operation is in the high performance coating subcategory of this subpart.
citations: 40 CFR 63.3981 (definition of High performance architectural coating)

criteria.criterion: If the metal components you coat are metal components of wood building products that meet the applicability criteria for wood building products surface coating (subpart QQQQ), then those metal-component coating operations are excluded from this subpart.

checklist: Is the part you coat a 'wood building product' (contains >50% by weight wood or wood fiber excluding glass and is used in construction)? (verify weight fraction and intended end use).

Are the coated items windows or window components, doors, millwork, moulding, or other items specifically listed under the wood building products subcategory? (verify product type against 63.4681(a)(1)).
Do you apply adhesives as part of finishing/laminating the wood products? (adhesives are treated as coatings under the wood NESHAP; verify adhesive use and function).
What is the annual volume of coatings used in the wood building products source category at this affected source (liters or gallons per year)? (compare to 4,170 L/yr threshold in 63.4681(b)).
Is the facility or affected source a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥10 tons/year of any single HAP or ≥25 tons/year of combined HAP)? (determine facility-level PTE).

Do any exclusions in 63.4681(c)(1)-(5) apply to your wood coating operations (e.g., part of plywood/composite wood manufacturing covered by another subpart, wood furniture manufacturing, prefabricated/mobile home production, noncommercial/hobby/research operations, or wood treatment by retort)?

For metal (aluminum) window components: are these metal components considered part of wood building products that meet subpart QQQQ applicability (if yes, MMMM may be excluded)? (verify how the metal components relate to the wood product and whether the overall product meets QQQQ criteria).

What is the annual volume of HAP-containing coatings used to coat miscellaneous metal parts at the facility (liters or gallons per year)? (compare to 946 L/yr threshold in 63.3881(b)); do coatings meet the 'non-HAP' criteria in 63.3981 if you are considering excluding them from the volume calculation).

Do the aluminum coatings meet the definition of high performance architectural coating (e.g., required to meet AAMA 605.2-2000)? (verify coating specifications and AAMA compliance to categorize under the high performance subcategory per 63.3881(a)(3) and 63.3981).

Are your coating application methods and supporting equipment part of an 'affected source' as defined (capture all coating operations, storage, mixing, conveyance, and waste-handling used for the coating activity)? (verify equipment list per 63.4682(b) for wood coatings and analogous coverage for metal coatings).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's note simply states both coatings are subject to QQQQ (wood window components) and MMMM (aluminum components). Our answer includes the key applicability criteria: QQQQ covers coatings/adhesives on products >50% wood used in building (including windows) and the relevant thresholds/exclusions; MMMM covers surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts (including aluminum components) and the high-performance subcategory, plus the exclusion for metal components of wood building products. These capture the reasons in the EPA notes."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Aerospace Manufacturing and Rework Facilities

criteria.criterion: If a facility produces, reworks, or repairs in any amount any aerospace vehicle or component and is a major source as defined in §63.2, then Subpart GG applies to the facility.
If a cleaning activity at the facility is a hand-wipe, spray gun cleaning, or flush cleaning operation, then that cleaning activity constitutes an affected source under this subpart.

If the cleaning operation is one of the operations listed in §63.744(e) (for example, cleaning of electronic parts and assemblies containing electronic parts or cleaning of aircraft fluid systems exposed to the fluid), then that cleaning operation is exempt from the hand-wipe cleaning requirements of §63.744(b).

If an activity is manufacture or rework of electronic parts and assemblies (except cleaning and topcoating of completed assemblies), or otherwise falls into the categories listed in §63.741(f), then those activities are not regulated by this subpart.

If a hand-wipe cleaning solvent meets one of the composition requirements in Table 1, or has a composite vapor pressure of 45 mm Hg or less at 20 °C, or the facility demonstrates a 60% reduction in hand-wipe solvent usage from an approved baseline, then the hand-wipe cleaning requirements of §63.744(b) are satisfied by those options.

If a spray gun cleaning operation is subject to this subpart, then compliance requires use of one or more of the techniques specified in §63.744(c)(1)–(4) (enclosed system, nonatomized cleaning, disassembled spray-gun cleaning, or atomizing cleaning with capture).

If cleaning solvent solutions contain organic HAP and VOC below the de minimis levels specified in §63.741(f), then those solvent solutions are exempt from the requirements in the referenced paragraphs of §63.744.

If an owner or operator is subject to Subpart GG for cleaning operations, then they must comply with the cleaning-specific recordkeeping requirements in §63.752(b) including maintaining solvent name, vapor pressure, organic HAP constituents, and usage records as applicable.

If a material used as a primer, topcoat, specialty coating, chemical milling maskant, stripper, or cleaning solvent meets the definition of “Non-HAP material” in §63.742, then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to that material (except as noted for averaging or recordkeeping when chosen).

candidates.title: General Provisions (as referenced by Subpart GG)

criteria.criterion: If an affected source is subject to Subpart GG, then the owner or operator is also subject to the General Provisions §§63.4, 63.5, and 63.6 as specified by Subpart GG unless otherwise excepted.

If an owner or operator requests an extension of compliance for an affected source under this subpart, then the request must be submitted not later than 120 days before the affected source's compliance date per the Subpart GG provisions that modify General Provisions timing.

If an owner or operator intends to use an air pollution control device or equipment not listed in Subpart GG, then they must submit a description, test data verifying performance, and operating parameters to the Administrator for approval not later than 120 days prior to the compliance date as required by Subpart GG.

checklist: Determine whether the facility is a major source under 40 CFR 63.2 (tons/year thresholds for single and combined HAP).
Confirm whether the facility performs manufacture or rework of aerospace vehicles or components (note: 'aerospace vehicle or component' definition at 40 CFR 63.742 excludes electronic components).
For each cleaning task, classify the operation type: hand-wipe, spray gun cleaning, or flush cleaning (per 40 CFR 63.741(c)(1)).

For each cleaning task, determine whether it matches any exemption in 40 CFR 63.744(e) (specifically: cleaning of electronic parts and assemblies and cleaning of aircraft fluid systems exposed to the fluid including hydraulic systems).
For solvents used (including azeotropic blends), obtain MSDS/product data and determine: organic HAP constituents and concentrations, VOC content, and composite vapor pressure at 20 °C.
Determine whether any cleaning solvent qualifies as a 'Non-HAP material' per 40 CFR 63.742 (and thus is excluded under 63.741(f)).

If using hand-wipe solvents, verify compliance path: meet Table 1 composition, meet ≤45 mm Hg vapor pressure at 20 °C, or document a 60% usage reduction from an approved baseline per 40 CFR 63.744(b).

If performing spray gun cleaning, document which §63.744(c) technique is used (enclosed system, nonatomized cleaning, disassembled cleaning, or atomizing cleaning with capture) and whether enclosed cleaners are leak-free per §63.744(c)(1)(ii).

Collect and retain the cleaning-operation records required by 40 CFR 63.752(b) (solvent name, vapor pressure, organic HAP constituents, monthly usage volumes, and records for exempt operations if applicable).

If planning to rely on averaging, use of non-listed control equipment, or seeking an extension, prepare required supporting data and submit applications/requests within the timeframes specified in 40 CFR 63.743 (e.g., 120 days for extension or control-device approval).

The criteria cite §63.741(f) and exempt categories, and the checklist requires classifying each cleaning task and checking exemptions (electronic parts/assemblies and aircraft fluid systems/hydraulic systems via §63.744(e)/§63.741(f)), so the EPA rationale is captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Petroleum Refineries (Subpart CC)

criteria.criterion: If the plant site is a major source as defined in CAA section 112(a) and the process units emit or contain one or more hazardous air pollutants listed in table 1, then this subpart applies to the petroleum refining process units and related emissions points at the plant site.

If a vent stream from a petroleum refining process unit contains greater than 20 parts per million by volume organic HAP, then that vent is a miscellaneous process vent and is within the affected source described in this subpart.

If the miscellaneous process vent meets the definition of a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent (total organic HAP concentration ≥20 ppmv and TOC emissions ≥ the applicable kg/day threshold at the outlet prior to control), then the owner/operator must comply with the Group 1 miscellaneous process vent requirements in §63.643 and the monitoring requirements in §63.644 unless another paragraph applies.

If the owner/operator chooses to reduce organic HAP emissions from a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent using a control device other than a flare, then the control device must achieve either a 98 weight-percent reduction of organic HAP or an outlet concentration of 20 parts per million by volume on a dry basis corrected to 3 percent oxygen, whichever is less stringent.

If the owner/operator proposes to use a boiler or process heater to meet the 98 percent reduction or 20 ppmv concentration requirement, then the vent stream must be introduced into the flame zone (or another location ensuring the required reduction/concentration is achieved) and testing/monitoring is required as specified in §63.644(a) and §63.645.

If the owner/operator of a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent uses a combustion device listed in §63.644(a) (incinerator, catalytic incinerator, flare, or boilers/process heaters per heat capacity rules), then the owner/operator must install and operate the monitoring equipment specified in §63.644(a)(1)–(4) unless exempted.

If the owner/operator seeks to monitor parameters other than those specified in §63.644(a), then the owner/operator may request approval to monitor alternative parameters by submitting a request in accordance with the procedures in §63.655(h).

If the process vent is used only as a result of startup, shutdown, maintenance, or inspection and meets the conditions in §63.643(c), then the owner/operator may designate it a maintenance vent and be required only to comply with the maintenance vent provisions in paragraph (c) (and the cited record/reporting provisions) for that vent.

If the vent system contains bypass lines that could divert the vent stream away from the control device, then the owner/operator must comply with one of the options in §63.644(c) (install hourly flow indicator/continuous valve position monitoring, secure the bypass with car-seal and monthly visual inspections, or use cap/blind flange/second valve per referenced standards).

checklist: Is the refinery plant site a major source under CAA section 112 (i.e., potential to emit ≥ major source thresholds)?
Does the orthoxylene rerun column vent stream contain >20 ppmv total organic HAP (measure vapor concentration) at the emission point prior to control?
What is the outlet total organic compound (TOC) or organic HAP emission rate at the outlet prior to control (kg/day) to determine Group 1 vs Group 2 status?
Is the orthoxylene rerun column part of a petroleum refining process unit assigned to the affected source at your plant site?
Is the vent routed to a refinery fuel gas system (and if so, are downstream flares subject to §63.670 compliance after Jan 30, 2019)?

Is the vent intended to be designated a maintenance vent and, if so, can you demonstrate one of the deinventory criteria in §63.643(c)(1)(i)–(v) (e.g., <10% LEL, ≤5 psig, <72 lb VOC, pyrophoric catalyst exception, or ≤2 psig after best practices)?

Which control device will be used (flare, thermal incinerator, catalytic incinerator, boiler, or process heater) and, for boilers/process heaters, what is the design heat input capacity (≥ or <44 megawatts)?
If using a boiler/process heater, will the vent stream be introduced into the flame zone (or other location demonstrated to meet required reduction/concentration)?
If using a flare, do you have continuous pilot flame monitoring per §63.644(a)(2) (or will you rely on §63.670 compliance for flares subject to that section)?
Are there bypass lines or valves that could divert the vent around the control device, and if so, which bypass control option from §63.644(c) will you implement and how will you document/monitor it?
Do you intend to monitor parameters other than those specified in §63.644(a); if so, are you prepared to submit an approval request per §63.655(h) with supporting rationale and monitoring plan?

Can the proposed control achieve the requested performance goal (either >98 wt% reduction or 20 ppmv dry corrected to 3% O2), and do you have test data or engineering justification to support establishing the operating range for the monitoring parameter(s) per §63.644(d)?

Prepare records needed for Notification of Compliance Status and Periodic Reports as applicable (e.g., monitoring ranges, performance test averages, continuous records for temperatures or pilot presence, bypass/diversion records) consistent with §63.644 and subpart CC reporting expectations.

candidates.title: National emission standards for hazardous waste combustors (Subpart EEE)

criteria.criterion: If an operating parameter limit is specified in § 63.1209, then you may apply to the Administrator to waive that operating parameter limit by documenting that neither that operating parameter limit nor an alternative operating parameter limit is needed to ensure compliance with the emission standards of this subpart.

If you request an alternative monitoring requirement or a waiver of an operating parameter limit, then you must submit the request no later than with the comprehensive performance test plan and include data justifying the request, a description of the proposed alternative monitoring or parameter, and data showing that the alternative would provide equivalent or better assurance of compliance.

If you prepare the comprehensive performance test plan, then you must include feedstream analysis that documents viscosity or a description of the physical form of each feedstream (so viscosity/physical-form information must be in the test plan even if you seek a waiver of an operating limit).

If your hazardous waste combustor has a hazardous waste firing system, then you must specify operating parameters and limits during the comprehensive performance test to ensure good operation of each hazardous waste firing system (i.e., firing-system OPLs are required under § 63.1209 unless waived via the application procedure).

If your source is equipped with a low-energy wet scrubber for hydrogen chloride/chlorine control, then you must establish a minimum liquid feed pressure (and/or minimum pressure drop) based on the manufacturer's specifications and comply with that limit on an hourly rolling average unless you obtain an approved waiver.

If you submit a waiver request for an operating parameter limit (for example for waste viscosity, feed/atomization pressure, or scrubber liquid feed pressure), then the Administrator will notify you of approval or intent to deny within the timeframes for alternative monitoring requests (notification within 90 calendar days after receipt and 60 days after supplementary information), and you remain responsible to provide timely supplementary information.

checklist: Confirm the unit is an affected hazardous waste combustor (hazardous waste incinerator) subject to Subpart EEE.
Identify the firing system type (fluidized bed with lance feed) and document where hazardous waste is introduced (feed locations) for the performance test plan.

Confirm which specific operating parameter limits were established previously or will be established in your Documentation/Notification of Compliance (e.g., waste viscosity, waste fuel delivery pressure, atomization pressure, minimum combustion chamber temperature, maximum hazardous waste feedrate, AWFCO interlocks).

Determine whether the HCl/Cl abatement is a wet scrubber and whether it is high-energy (venturi, etc.) or low-energy (spray tower, packed bed, tray tower) to know whether minimum liquid feed pressure or pressure-drop OPLs apply (and locate manufacturer specs).
Prepare comprehensive performance test plan feedstream analyses that include viscosity or a description of the physical form for each feedstream (per § 63.1207(f)(1)(i)).

Assemble data to justify a waiver: emissions data, performance-test data, process/engineering rationale, alternative monitoring descriptions, and demonstration that the alternative provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance.

Plan to submit any waiver/alternative-monitoring application together with the comprehensive performance test plan (timing is required), and be ready to supply any supplemental information promptly during review.

Document how the proposed waiver would maintain required safety and AWFCO interlocks and how omission of a particular monitored parameter would not prevent automatic waste feed cutoff or other required protective actions.

Verify manufacturer specifications for scrubber minimum liquid feed pressure and be prepared to show why monitoring this parameter is unnecessary or provide an alternative that ensures equivalent control.
Be prepared to update the Notification of Compliance and operating requirements if the Administrator approves a waiver or alternative monitoring approach.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Iron and Steel Foundries

criteria.criterion: If your foundry is an existing affected source, then you must be in compliance with each applicable emissions limitation, work practice standard, and O&M requirement no later than April 23, 2007.

If you are required to conduct a performance test to demonstrate initial compliance, then you must conduct that performance test no later than 180 calendar days after the compliance date specified in § 63.7683.

If you intend to use a performance test as your initial compliance demonstration (including a test performed before the compliance date), then the test must be conducted under conditions representative of normal operations (not during startup, shutdown, or malfunction) and must include process information documenting that representativeness.

If you conducted a PM performance test for a pouring area or pouring station, then the test must follow the PM test methods and procedures in § 63.7732(b) (including required sampling methods, minimum sample volume, and at least three valid test runs) to be acceptable.

If you use a performance test to demonstrate initial compliance for a pouring area at an existing foundry, then the average PM concentration (per § 63.7732(b)) must not exceed 0.010 gr/dscf or the average total metal HAP concentration (per § 63.7732(c)) must not exceed 0.0008 gr/dscf to meet the initial compliance criteria.

If you conducted a performance test, then you must have provided a notification of intent to conduct the performance test at least 60 calendar days before the test date and must submit the notification of compliance status (including performance test results) no later than 60 calendar days after completion of the performance test.

If you will rely on a prior performance test as your initial compliance demonstration, then you must have records of the operating parameter data measured during the performance test (and any site-specific operating limits established from that test) as required for establishing and demonstrating operating limits.

checklist: Is the foundry an existing affected source (operating before the relevant new-source date) or a new source (check startup date relative to April 22, 2004)? (40 CFR 63.7683)
What was the date(s) of the April 2005 stack/PM test for the M-1 Pouring Area?
Was a Notification of Intent to conduct the performance test submitted at least 60 days before the April 2005 test? (40 CFR 63.7750(d))
Were at least three valid test runs completed and was a minimum sample volume of 60 dscf collected for each PM sampling run as required? (40 CFR 63.7732(b)(2))

Were the April 2005 test runs conducted during conditions representative of normal operations (not during startup, shutdown, or malfunction) and is there written process information documenting that representativeness? (40 CFR 63.7732(a))

For each test run, are records available of metal charged, test duration, stack flow rate, and other process parameters needed to calculate mass-based emission rates (lb/ton) if applicable? (40 CFR 63.7732(b)(6), (c)(6))

Do the April 2005 test results meet the numeric initial compliance criteria for a pouring area at an existing foundry (average PM ≤ 0.010 gr/dscf or average total metal HAP ≤ 0.0008 gr/dscf)? (40 CFR 63.7734(a)(5))
Was the notification of compliance status including the performance test results submitted within 60 days after completion of the April 2005 test? (40 CFR 63.7750(e)(2))

Were any site-specific operating limits established from the test and are the operating parameter data recorded during the performance test retained to support those limits? (40 CFR 63.7734(b)(1)(i)-(ii))

Are the production rates (metal charged per unit time) during the April 2005 test the same as or adequately representative of your current production capability and normal operating cycles for the M-1 Pouring Area? (40 CFR 63.7732(a), 63.7732(b)(4)-(6))

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Yes. The EPA’s two key reasons—(1) test runs must collect at least 60 dscf per §63.7732(b)(2) (the April 2005 runs were only 47–49 dscf), and (2) prior tests are acceptable only if production rates/operations are representative per §63.7732(a)—are explicitly included in the answer’s criteria and checklist (citations to §63.7732(a) and §63.7732(b)(2) are present)."}

candidates.title: Mercury cell chlor-alkali production facilities

criteria.criterion: If you operate by-product hydrogen streams or end box ventilation system vents at a mercury cell chlor-alkali production facility, then you must determine weekly mercury emission rates and reduce them to a 52-week average expressed in g Hg/Mg Cl2 to demonstrate continuous compliance.

If you operate a mercury thermal recovery unit vent and you choose the continuous monitoring option under §63.8240(a), then you must calculate the daily average mercury concentration for each operating day using 15-minute CEM readings per Equation 2.

If you operate a mercury thermal recovery unit vent and you choose the periodic monitoring option under §63.8240(b), then you must calculate the daily average mercury concentration using the procedures in §63.8234(b).

If you choose the continuous monitoring option for an affected source, then you must sample, analyze, and record mercury concentration at least once every 15 minutes and exclude data recorded during monitoring malfunctions, associated repairs, and required QA/QC from averages and availability calculations.

If you choose the periodic monitoring option and your final control device is not a nonregenerable carbon adsorber, then you must install and operate a CPMS that continuously collects data at least once every 15 minutes and records each 1-hour average for the applicable parameters as specified.

If you are using continuous monitoring to demonstrate compliance for by-product hydrogen streams or end box ventilation system vents, then the mercury CEM data used to compute averages must represent at least 75 percent of the 15-minute periods in each operating day of the 52-week compliance period.

If you choose the continuous mercury monitoring option, then the mercury continuous emissions monitor analyzer must have a detector capable of detecting either 0.1 µg/m3 or 0.5 times the mercury concentration measured during the performance test.

checklist: Identify each affected vent: list which are by-product hydrogen streams, which are end box ventilation vents, and which (if any) are mercury thermal recovery unit vents.
Decide and document the monitoring option for each affected vent: continuous (§63.8240(a)) or periodic (§63.8240(b)).
If continuous is chosen: confirm CEM samples/records at least once every 15 minutes and that the analyzer meets the detection capability (0.1 µg/m3 or 0.5× performance-test level).

If continuous is chosen: confirm data availability meets the ≥75% of 15-minute periods per operating day requirement for 52-week averaging (for by-product H2/end box vents) or per operating day for thermal recovery units.

If periodic is chosen: determine whether the final control device is a nonregenerable carbon adsorber (different periodic procedures apply) and, if not, ensure a CPMS is installed that collects data at least once every 15 minutes and records 1‑hour averages for the applicable parameters.

For by-product hydrogen/end box vents: record weekly mercury emission rates and weekly chlorine production and be prepared to calculate 52-week averages (first 52-week average begins at the compliance-date-specified start).

For mercury thermal recovery unit vents: if using continuous monitoring, implement calculation of daily-average concentration from the 15-minute readings (Equation 2); if using periodic monitoring, identify and be prepared to follow the procedures in §63.8234(b).
Maintain records of weekly, daily, hourly (if applicable), and 52-week average values and all required QA/QC, monitoring malfunctions, repairs, and corrective actions as required by the subpart.

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you seek approval to change or set operating limits or other compliance parameters not specified in §§63.2455 through 63.2485 (including recordkeeping approaches that redefine operating scenarios), then you must submit a precompliance report requesting approval as specified in 40 CFR 63.2520(c).

If your process includes batch process vents, then you must keep a schedule or log of operating scenarios for batch operations and update it each time a different operating scenario is put into effect.

If you are subject to a percent reduction emission limit in Table 2 and some Group 1 batch process vents are controlled to less than the percent reduction requirement, then you must keep records of whether each batch operated was considered a standard batch and estimate uncontrolled and controlled emissions for each batch that is considered a nonstandard batch.

If you documented in your notification of compliance status that total uncontrolled organic HAP emissions from the batch process vents in an MCPU will be less than 1,000 lb/yr for the anticipated number of standard batches, then you must keep records of the number of batches operated and calculate a daily rolling annual sum of batches operated no less frequently than monthly; if you did not document that, you must maintain the more detailed per-batch or daily emissions records specified in paragraph (e)(4).

If you elect to comply via emissions averaging instead of individual percent reduction limits, then you may follow the emissions averaging provisions in §63.150 as modified by this subpart (including using the standard-batch emissions estimation method in §63.1257(d)(2)(i) and (ii) for batch vents when calculating monthly debits and credits).

If you propose to rely on engineering assessments, alternative emissions calculations, or to change how a condenser is treated (e.g., control device vs process condenser) for initial compliance or recordkeeping, then you must include the data, rationale, and descriptions in the precompliance report or notification of compliance status as required by 40 CFR 63.2520(c) and 63.2520(d).

If you change any of the operating-scenario elements specified in §63.2525(b) that were previously reported (except paragraph (b)(5)), then that change constitutes a new operating scenario and must be reported in the next compliance report with the information specified in §63.2525(b).

If you use the terms standard batch or nonstandard batch to define emissions for recordkeeping or averaging, then you must apply the definitions and requirements for standard batch, nonstandard batch, and operating scenario contained in the subpart and keep per-batch or per-scenario records as required by this subpart.

checklist: Determine whether the affected vents are batch process vents as defined in 40 CFR 63.2550 (identify vents manifolded to common headers, reactors, condensers, process tanks, etc.).
Calculate uncontrolled organic HAP emissions per batch and sum per process to determine Group 1 vs Group 2 status (use procedures referenced in §63.2460(b) and §63.1257(d)(2)(i)/(ii)).
Verify whether any percent reduction emission limit in Table 2 to subpart FFFF applies to your process and whether emissions averaging is intended to be used.

Decide whether your current operating scenarios and standard-batch definitions (operating-condition ranges and emissions-per-standard-batch) are documented and whether you plan to change them or to define multiple standard batches for reporting purposes.

If relying on reduced/alternative recordkeeping, prepare a precompliance report package per 40 CFR 63.2520(c) including requested approvals, descriptions of operating scenarios, test conditions/data/calculations supporting the proposed approach, and any engineering assessments.

Check whether you have submitted or will submit the Notification of Compliance Status and whether it already documents any assumptions (e.g., Group 2 status, non-reactive HAP <10,000 lb/yr) that affect recordkeeping per 40 CFR 63.2520(d) and 63.2525(e).

Confirm the frequency and method you will use to calculate and retain monthly rolling annual sums (batches or emissions) to align with inventory and SARA 313 reporting (e.g., monthly calculation per 40 CFR 63.2525(e)(2)/(3)).

Identify all elements of §63.2525(b) (process description, vents included, control devices, monitoring/parametric levels, calculations/analyses) that would be affected by redefining standard batches and prepare to report any changes as new operating scenarios per 40 CFR 63.2525(b)(8) and 63.2520(e)(7).
